I think the hon. minister who has this Bill in charge has not given consideration to it in all its bearings.
It seems to me he has altogether failed to consider the cases of certain producers on the Pacific coast who are being oppressed now by a combine created by the hon. gentleman himself, and that we are having a repetition of what we saw in the House the other day, namely, the government being exempted from the operation of a veLV benign law. I do not see why we should pass a Bill here interfering with private citizens in the conduct of their business and expresslv exempting -a combine fostered and maintained by the government of Canada.
Where is the combine?
The combine is the fishery combine.
How does it operate?

I have very much pleasure in explaining to the minister how ft operates, and I am sure the story wil excite his compassion, and cause him to make an amendment such as I have suggested. We have, as the minister knows, on the Pacific coast the sole source of sup-nlv for the sockeye salmon, that is tne salmon that is canned. We have a regula-lation of the Fisheries Department whereby no persons who are not already in the business of canning salmon are able to obtain salmon canning licenses, the theory upon which that prohibition is based being that there are already a sufficient number of persons engaged in that industry, and that to increase the number would affect the supply. We have the natural result that all persons in that industry have formed themselves into an absolutely tight combine, a combine ranging not only through Canada, but extending to the adjoining portions of the United States, where they catch the salmon in very considerable quantities. This government protects that combine so far as Canada is concerned by further enacting that no Canadian fisherman catching fish in Canada shall be allowed to export those fish. His market is restarted to the market offered by the canners in the combine on the Canadian side. He must sell to them. If he does not sell to them, he must destroy his fish. The operation of that last year, for instance, brought about this condition of affairs, that whilst the canners on the Canadian side and on the American side are buying the identical fish, canning bv the same process, at even cost, selling in the same market, under their combination which fixes the selling price both in Canada and the United States, our Canadian canners combined to make the price of fish in Canada 10 cents per fish, while a few miles away on the American

side, fish were selling at 20 cents a fish. Therefore, this combine operated to deprive the Canadian fishermen of half the earnings last summer to which they were entitled.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman to want a law put through which would compel the fishermen to sell the fish at double the price they are selling at the present time, a law to make fish dearer to every one who wants to purchase fish in British Columbia?
The minister asks a question worthy of a tyro in public affairs. I do not think I am called upon to answer any question of that kind.
Do not misunderstand my question. I understood the hon. gentleman to state that the effect of this combine in British Columbia was to keep down the price at which fish were sold.
The price at which the poor fishermen are obliged to sell them.

I may explain to the minister that this combine which he as a member of the government has assisted to create and is assisting to maintain, and which he could wipe out in five minutes by altering one or two orders in council, has *effect of cutting down the price at which the fish caught in the Fraser river would otherwise be saleable.
Is not that an advantage to the consumer ?

No, it is not, because the consumer in eastern Canada Pi?^S *tlle [DOT] I)T:'ce	in conjunction with
x ji American canners, who on their side of "the line pay 20 cents per fish as against 10 cents on our side; so that the consumer is paying on the 20 cent basis.

I think the hon. gentleman does not understand the working of his own combine. If he did, I think he would cause it to cease to exist. My complaint in this case is not on behalf of the consumer, although I think the consumer has a just cause of complaint. I am speaking as the member for New Westminster, where the producers of the fish work who are deprived of half the revenue to which they are entitled from the sale of those fish because of the operation of the canning combine, and I am asking the minister to include in this Bill a provision whereby we can set the machinery of the department in operation and prove beyond the possibility of cavil that the effect of the combine of the salmon canners is to reduce the price to the producers of fish to 250*
one-half of what they would otherwise get, while it does not benefit the consumers in any way. On the contrary, the consumers are charged as much for these fish as they are for the American fish for which double the price is paid. The minister can afford us relief in any one of three ways: he can give us a chance to come under the operation of this Act and allow any fishermen detrimentally affected to make application for investigation just as consumers can ; or he can persuade his colleagues to remove the prohibition of the export of fish; or he can persuade them to remove the prohibition of persons not now engaged in the canning industry to go into it, so that we may at least have competition on the part of capital. Not only are these fishermen deprived of half their livelihood on the fish they sell, but they are deprived of the right to sell a large portion of the fish they catch when the run is large; because when they go to the Canadian canneries after a night when they have caught say 400 fish to the boat, they find a notice put up by the canners that on account of the large run the canners will take only say 200 fish per boat. The result is that a man who has 400 fish to sell can sell only 200 of them, because this government prohibits him exporting them across the line, where the American canners would be glad to take them at a higher price; so that he is obliged either to dump them into the river, which also is against the law, or to go ashore and dig a great hole and bury them, which of course no one would do. If the minister is sincere in his effort to deal with combines in a way to bring undoubted benefit to the people of Canada"! he will not tell these poor fishermen that they must wait for another year or perhaps two years before he will give them relief.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had stated the whole case, my hon. colleague and the House would appreciate the situation betteT. To some extent it is true that the fishery regulations on the Pacific coast, as on the Atlantic coast, have created more or less of a combine; that is, the number of canners is limited and the number of fishing licenses is limited. The provincial government at the present moment is limiting the number of boats which may be licensed to fish, a certain number to each cannery. All this is done for the purpose of conserving the fish in the waters of British Columbia. The particular point to which my hon. friend refers is that the fishing on the bays or rivers of British Columbia is carried on by individual fishermen. Probably as many as 4,000 boats have licenses to fish in the Fraser river and estuary. Immediately south of the boundary line, not more than about 30 miles away are hundreds of American

traps for the supply of the American can-ners. There is very little gill netting as compared with trap fishing. Some years ago the cannery men on the Fraser river, when short of fish completed their packing operations for the dav or the week by bringing fish taken in traps south of the boundary line, and I can remember very well that the Canadian fishermen licensed to catch fish on the Fraser river objected to the free importation of fisfi from Washington State 30 or 40 miles away from the supply of the British Columbia canners. I do not know whether a duty was then put on fbh or not. I am not sure about that, but the department some years ago prohibited the bringing in of fish to be canned in the canneries. What for? In the interests of the cannery men? Not at all, but in the interests of the fishermen of the Fraser river. Necessarily that regulation had to be reciprocal, and fish foT the purpose of being canned were prohibited.
Now', if it were possible for the Canadian fishermen to sell their fish, not to the cannery men for whom they are catch. ing, hut to the United States cannery men, when the prices south of the line may be a little more than those north of the line, it would be the proper thing for the canners on the Fraser river to go down and buy fish taken in the American traps. But this has been prohibited, and I think it is in the interests of the fishermen of the Fraser river. The arrangement, I think, has worked fairly satisfactorily. I do not think the prices that my hon. friend speaks about are fairly stated. Ten cents a fish on the Fraser river, my hon. friend knows perfectly well, has been exceeded time and again; it goes up as high as 20 cents and 25 cents a fish, particularly when there is a scarcity. When there is a big run, which sometimes happens, when a fisherman may come_ m with 400 or 500 fish, and it is impossible for the canneries to take care of all the fish for the next twenty-four hours, half of them have to be thrown away. That seldom happens now, but it has happened, and as a result the price drops, and it might come down to even 10 cents. But to state to this House that the price paid by the Fraser river canneries is 10 cents a fish, and on the other side of the line 20 cents a fish, is not stating the case fairly or accurately. It is a reciprocal arrangement, initiated because the fishermen protested against the cannery men buying fish south of the line. It must be remembered also, as I stated a moment ago, that all the fish caught in the Fraser river, are caught by individual fishermen. There are no traps in the Fraser river. We have four or five times the number of fishermen engaged in catching fish that they have in the state of Washington, although the state Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
of Washington puts up more fish than we do. I believe this is not a matter for the Bill regulating combines. It is matter for the fishery regulations of the Marine and Fisheries Department. Any regulation made for the limitation of the number of canneries that may be erected must necessarily create more or less of a combine, a combine in the sense that the number is limited, that is all. The cannery men on the Fraser river, when fixing the price to be paid for fish during the season get together_ and agree as to how much they are going to pay, but as soon as the fish gets scarce, they have to increase their price. There is that arrangement I have referred to. in regard to the importation or exportation of fish, and it seems to me impossible to do anything in connection with that under this Bill.

I think the acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries, like the Minister of Labour, is speaking without knowledge of the subject. I would like to ask him in what form is the prohibition of the importation of fish, whether it is under the Customs Act or is part of the Fisheries regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My recollection- Is that it is part of the Fisheries regulations, but I am not certain. It has been in force for some years, the issuing of licenses, for instance, to cannery men, has, I think, the stipulation that the fish caught under the license must be canned in Canada.

I had a copy of the regulations here with which I think I could very easily confound the minister, but .unfortunately I have mislaid it, and in "the absence of the copy, I will not say anything as to a point on which I have at the moment no positive information. But I wish to say to the minister that he totally misunderstands the situation created by this combine. It is not a matter of chance, whether the fish shall be dear to-day or cheap to-morrow. As he ought to know, the cannery men at the beginning of the season, some weeks in advance of the opening, get together and lay down a definite price as they did last year. I do not hke the minister to stand up in this chirpy manner and tell the House that I have made a statement which is not correct. If there is one subject on which I am informed, having reference to the interests of my constituency, it is that of the salmon fishery, and when I made the statement as to that fishery, I made a statement that is absolutely and entirely correct, which conceals nothing, and upon the correctness of which I am prepared to stake my reputation. Now, I say that last year our Canadian canners met and fixed the prices at 10 cents per fish up to a certain time,

and a price of 12} cents per fish up to a certain time later.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I don't dispute that fact at all.

That arrangement was not made casually, but was the result of long discussion, creating a great deal of heart-burning among the Canadian fishermen. As to the price on the American side, I have equally precise information, that while our men had to sell at 10 cents, the price to the same combine buying on the American side was 20 cents, and that while the Canadian fishermen had to sell at 12} cents, the combine on the other side was paying 25 cents. I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I have a statement from an American source showing those prices, paid for the enormous catch made on the American side. I am sure that the fishermen on the Fraser river will be greatly surprised and disappointed when they find that the minister, whom they regard as their special custodian, is opposed to the suggestion I have made here, or has advised his colleague not to do something in this Act to enable the fishermen on the Fraser river to get the prices they are entitled to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is absolutely unnecessary to suggest an amendment to this Act. If it is an improper thing to have this prohibition of Canadian fish from being canned on the other side, and the prohibition of the importation of American trap-caught salmon, to be canned on the Fraser river, it can be amended by repealing the regulation. I am not speaking by the book when I say that it is part of the fisheries regulations. I tried to explain the matter as I understood it from the knowledge I gained some six years ago. It has not been under discussion for some time, and I cannot even say I ever read the regulation. But I heard it explained at the time, and I think the prohibition referred to is part of the regulation. However, there is a prohibition of that kind, and there is no disputing the fact as to the price. I quite agree that the cannery men do get together and they do fix the price they are going to pay, it may be from 10 cents upwards, and they do negotiate with the fishermen, the fishermen, of course, wanting a higher price. A fair price so much depends on the run of fish, which nobody knows anything about until the fish actually come. Prices have sometimes started high and dropped, and they have started low and risen.
Will the hon. minister permit me a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There can be no controversy as to this matter
If the hon. minister will permit me, I would like to ask him how the price can depend on the run of fish, if the canners fix it ahead of the coming of the fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is one of the problematical things they must take into account in fixing the price-it is one of the uncertainties of the trade. The hon. member (Mr. Burrell) knows that we have about an average run of fish. When we used to have every fourth year a big year, the price was low.
I understood my hon. friend from New Westminster to say that the price was not regulated by an antecedent act of a combine, but regulated from time to time actually by the run of the fish.

In connection with the suggestion of the hon. member for Pic-tou (Mr. MacDonald) to allow this Act to apply only to combines against consumers, and not against producers, I think the hon. member omits a very large class of the community-in fact, I think a larger class is affected by combines than the other, especially in agricultural produce. There is scarcely an agricultural product that must not be sold to a combine-in practice only a combine buys it. A combine of wheat buyers .buys the wheat; a combine of fruit buyers, buys the fruit; the dairy products are bought by a combine; and the same is true of beef, pofk, mutton, and other meats. I have looked forward to this Bill as being a very useful one for our community at (all events. I think, therefore, that, in the general interest, the hon. member for Pictou should withdraw his suggestion and allow the Bill to apply to combines against the producers as well as to combines against consumers.

I think that, possibly, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sealey) does; not follow the effect of a combine quite far enough. If I understood him rightly, his contention is that certain products are bought by combines who buy at a low figure, that they may control the market. Surely, the resultant effect -would be shown upon those who purchase from the combine. It -certainly would affect the consumer of the article, and if it did, the Bill would apply. I think, that if the hon. member looks carefully at the law1, he will see that, in the last analysis-, the purchaser of the article in question must be affected, and if it affects the purchaser then this measure will applv. .
In connection with that, it does not seem that it will quite applv, or that it has applied in the past.
We had not the law in the past.

But we have had the evil, although the law to remedy it has not toeen in existence. Take the matter of pork, for instance. On March 16, 1908, pork was sold at $4.90 per hundred weight, or practically five cents per pound, on foot, and the retail price of bacon here in the Ottawa stores was 22 cents. To-day, pork is $9.50 to $10 per hundred weight, on foot, and bacon is offered right here at 22 cents per pound. At present, the consumer is, perhaps, getting it _ at about a proper proportion to the price that the producer receives. But, two years ago, the producer was getting only half the money and the consumer did not get the product any cheaper. The producers in our country did make an effort to get the provincial government to act in order to prevent the combine paying an unfair price to the producer. But the matter was not even effectually started, because the provincial law seemed so difficult and complicated, and the officers in charge did not appear to be very persistent in pushing the matter. Therefore, as I have said, I have looked forward to this law as being of great assistance to the agricultural producers. If the consumer had then appealed against the unfair price he -was being charged, he could have succeeded to some extent, but he could not have completely succeeded as against the combines that were forcing prices down. At that time, they were working on this basis: Everybody knows that our neighbours to the south have a very large production of food products, and they have, on the exchange in 'Chicago, what they call a bull day and a bear day. The market is bulled up for twenty-five days in the month, and the other day the bears are on top. In that way, the packers' combine were able to buy at an average of about 'three cents less than the average market value. They could pay the two cents duty charged by the Canadian customs, sell in Canada and still be one cent ahead of the game. And everybody knows that, looking at it from the point of view of the producer when the hog is brought to about 200 pounds, he must be sold irrespective of price. So, they were able to keep the farmers down to hard pan, or even below, and still make a high charge to the consumer. As against the contention of the minister, the fact that the price of bacon to the consumer is the same as it was when the packers were allowing the producer only half the price seems to me to be conclusive. Many other instances might be given of agricultural products that are handled in the same way as pork. I think that it will be a great gain to Canada as a whole to pursue the combines from the producer's as Mr. SEALEY.
well as from the consumer's standpoint. However, it will be a great benefit and advantage to have them prevented -from wrongfully taking advantage of either class.

Under this section, 'Combine' means any contract, &c., which has or is designed to have the effect of increasing or fixing the price or rental of any article of trade, cost of storage, &c., 'to the detriment of consumers'. Of course, any increase, reasonable or unreasonable, may be said to be to the detriment of consumers. I would suggest that the minister put in words to make it read 'which has or is designed to have the effect of unreasonably increasing or fixing the price', and, in the fifth line, 'or of unduly restricting competition'-insert the words 'unreasonably' and; 'unduly'.

I would point out to the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) that this is simply a definition. The law itself applies rather to the effects of combines than to combines as such. I think it very desirable that the definition should be as broad as possible, so that all classes of combinations may be brought under the operation of the law. I quite agree that it would not be proper to have any one rendered liable simply for taking part in the formation of a combine as such. But, if when the combine formed unduly or unreasonably enhances prices, it is quite proper that the parties interested should be proceeded against under this measure. If the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) will look at section 7, he will find that, before an examination can be ordered, the judge must be satisfied that it is in the public interest that that investigation should take place, and that the combination that exists is injurious to trade or has operated to the detriment of consumers generally. I think it would be hardly wise to include debatable words in the definition. For that reason I would not care to add the words suggested to the definition. I have no objection to having the Act safeguard any applications to the judge so as to prevent parties being harassed in an unfair manner; but I do not think it would be wise to put debatable words into the definition.

Would the minister tell us why he does not include the farmers as well as the consumers, in accordance with the suggestions made by my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Sealey), so that ip may apply to combines which stand between the farmers and the consumers?

I have carefully considered that point. I think I have mentioned that any combination, if it is going to be a vital factor in the process at all, will in the last analysis reveal its effect in the prices

of the article as sold in the market, and in that way consumers would be affected by a combine. Further, I may point out that, as I have already said, this legislation is in some particulars a departure, and I think it is desirable that we should proceed perhaps not too rapidly at the outset. If, after the law has been on the statutes for a year, it is found that it works well to the extent to which it does apply, and that producers have a grievance which cannot be remedied under it as it stands at present, it would be easy to make the necessary amendments and to enlarge the scope of the Act. But I think it would be wise to see whether, in the first instance, the law as it is now framed is not broad enough to meet the case which has been suggested.
What kind of a position would the farmer be in? He is a producer, and he would not be able to make any complaints, he would have to wait until the consumer made the complaints.

The representations that have come to the government so far from different sources, have been almost wholly in regard to combines against consumers. The question of the effect of combines on producers is being raised now for the first time, that is to say, to any extent, I think all the communications that have been received and the representations that have been made to the government, have been in respect to consumers, not as respects producers. But, as my hon. friend will see while every farmer is a producer of one article, he is a consumer of a thousand or more. Looking at the matter from the point of view of his being a consumer of articles of food and clothing, and everything needed for his household and his farm generally, to all of which classes of articles this law applies particularly, it will be apparent that the farmer would be the man of all men who Will reap great advantage from this legislation. I might further point out that in the letter from the Master of the Grange, which I read on the second reading of the Bill, the writer stated the the Grange had carefully considered this Bill and that members of the Grange were enthusiastically in favour of the measure, and wished it to pass at the present session. But nothing was said in that communication in regard to enlarging the scope of the Bill in the manner which has been suggested.
The minister understands the position of the farmer. The farmer may sell his products to a combine m that line, land yet he has no recourse under this Act.

After reading this Act and listening to the discussions upon it, I do not think it will have the desired effect,
either upon the consumer or the producer. The Minister of Labour said a few moments ago that there wa3 some protection given to the producer by way of a special tariff, but if the tariff is only a revenue tariff, I do not see how it can protect any one. I do not see how the tariff is going to protect the man who raises pigs on a farm or the man who raises beef, and I do not understand how it will protect the man who catches fish on the Atlantic coast. The Minister of Inland Revenue said a moment ago that the lessening of the number of licenses issued to canners would be a protection to the fishery. Did anybody ever _ hear that lessening the number of canning licenses was going to protect the fish in the sea, when you let the same number of people go out to catch them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman understands that if you lessen the number of licensees who are authorized to catch fish, you are thereby lessening the number of fishermen?

If I didn't know any more about fishing then the Minister of Inland Revenue, I wouldn't attempt to say anything about it. From what he has said, I have come to the conclusion that he knows very little about the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast, and probably on the Pacific coast either. In the east the only licenses we have are licenses to can lobsters, and those licenses have been limited. But the methods of catching lobsters have not been limited, nor has the numbeT of men going into lobster fishing been limited either. The number of boat3 has not been limited, but the number of canning licenses has been unduly limited. But the Fisheries Committee have taken that matter up, and have shown that they do not desire any such combination as that. But in all these matters we are speaking only of the consumers of the articles and not of the producers. Take my own province of Nova Scotia. We have there a large fresh fish industry, but by virtue of the cold storage system which has been established by the government, the fishermen are not getting fair play. The fisherman goes out and catches fresh fish, and in consequence of the cold storage system the price of fish has been greatly reduced. People engaged in the cold storage business make an arrangement by which they buy so much fish, and I am sorry to say, at a very small price, running from half a cent a pound to two cents a pound. You cannot buy fresh fish anywhere in the eastern part of Canada of the same class of fish for less than about 10 cents a pound. Now, who gets the difference, where does it go to? There should be some method by which these fishermen may call for an investigation to see whether they are getting a fair and reasonable price for their fish

that they have to sell from half a cent up to two cents a pound. Half a cent to two cents a pound is not a fair price for fresh fish retailing in the vicinity of ten cents a pound and upwards. I can understand the Minister, of Labour saying that we will try this Act for one year, and if it works well, we will enlarge it next year. This is something which has been going on for a long time, and if it is possible we should make some effort to deal with it. The minister says that everybody is a consumer and that consequently this Bill will help everybody. If a man cannot produce, he cannot consume, because he cannot find the money to buy. He has to produce first in order to get the wherewithal to buy. I would be very glad to have a law placed upon the statute-book that would provide a fair means of regulation as between the producer and the consumer. I am speaking more particularly on behalf of the men who produce the raw material. The man in the coal mines is not protected. He has no opportunity of saying how much per ton he shall get for the coal he mines, while the coal company is getting so much per ton at the pit head. I notice that under the Bill as it is proposed to be amended, the six persons who make application-

speechtext: I think I will have to ask the hon. gentleman to confine himself to what is before the committee. It is the definition of the word ' combine.' The section that the hon. gentleman wishes to enter upon is section 5.
If you rule that I cannot discuss that part of the clause I will defer what I have to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not wish to be arbitrary, but for the sake of regularity I think the hon. gentleman might wait until we go back to section 5.

I understood the minister to make the statement that he had received no representations from producers that certain combines were injuring them. In answer to that I might draw his attention to the fact that the small tanners, who are producers, applied to the government to intercede or do something which would enable them to sell their product without restraint. It was not from the consumers that the application came, but from the producers, the small tanners all over the country who were either compelled to enter into an agreement, that they 'would buy their supplies from certain firms or otherwise they could not sell any leather to these firms. The product which they had was thereby reduced in value, and the sale circumscribed very much on account of that arrangement.

In answer to the hon. gentleman I would point out that the complaint was that the combination of certain tanners was in restraint of trade, and that it was operating to the detriment of the consumers. If it was really a combine maintained for the purpose of preventing people from buying their goods outside it would be covered by this Bill. Similarly, my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) has been speaking of a combination in regard to fish. A ' combine/ as defined in this Bill, means a combination for restricting competition in or controlling the production of certain articles. The definition is pretty broad. If a combine controls the production of or restricts competition in any article by any kind of an agreement it will come within the definition of the word ' combine ' as herein set forth.

Will the minister tell me how fishermen, who have been selling their fish to those who have cold storage facilities can bring about an investigation into the question of the price that they sell their fish at, as well as the price at which the purchasers resell the fish?

If the persons interested in cold storage were restricting the supply' of fish in any way that would be a combine, and the effect of the restriction would be to the detriment of the consumer. _ If it were shown that there was a combination amongst cold storage men, or any other group who were operating in a manner to restrict trade, an investigation could be had under this Act. If it were shown that there was no such combination I do not see that the question of fixing the price on the part of the men who were selling the fish would actually come in because there would be absolute freedom of competition, and they could sell to whomsoever they wished as a result of that competition and freedom.	.

There are a number of cold storage men who handle fresh fish. These men get together and say they will pay so much for fish to-day, and so much during the season. They do not restrict the production of fish at all; they take all the fish that the fishermen give them. When the fishermen get sufficient fish, and bring it into Canso, where there are two or three concerns who buy fish, they give them a certain price-from half a cent to two cents a pound-very seldom going to two cents a pound-and they resell that fish in Nova Scotia at not less than ten cents a pound. There should be some method by which the fishermen could show that they were not being treated fairly or reasonably, that these people pay a certain price and then resell to the consumer at a much higher price.

I do not think we have any need to go any farther than the hon. gentleman's own statement. He alleges that this combination of cold storage dealers arrange prices, and that after paying a certain price they sell at another price in virtue of the combine which the hon. gentleman says exists.

I am not worrying particularly about the price at which they sell to the public, hut what I am particularly worried about is the price that the fishermen get from the purchasers wlm have the cold storage facilities. These men have been assisted in providing these facilities by grants from the public treasury, and they have been put in a position to enable them to handle this fresh fish business. I have no doubt that the government intended also when assisting to provide these facilities that the fisherman should be helped. But help is not given to the fisherman because he simply has to sell his fish at the price offered him. The buyers take all the fish they can get; they do not curtail production at all. I do not know whether I have made myself clear to the minister.

I quite understand the contention of the hon. member (Mr. Crosby) although I have not heard very much complaint in that direction. His complaint appears to be that this is a combine to keep down prices.

I am speaking of keeping down the price as far as purchasing from the fisherman is concerned, but when the fish goes into the hands of the merchant immediately the price goes up. I desire the fisherman to get a much better price or a chance to regulate it.

It is a combine to prevent the fishermen from getting a better price for his goods. If there is a combine of that kind and it can be prevented it would be a very proper thing to do. The fishermen in the district that I am best acquainted with have not made very many complaints of that kind to me. There are always a large number of buyers on the coast and if one will not buy another will. As the hon. gentleman has said that the cold storage places may have been to some extent oppressive, I think that would be a very proper subject of investigation when we are giving them a subsidy. There is no reason .why a cold storage concern which obtains a subsidy from this government should be allowed to oppress the fishermen with whom they deal. I do not say they have done so. There ought to be some way for the government to investigate a matter of that kind so as to see that the seller to these cold storage concerns subsidized by the government should get fair play. I understand that the hon. gentleman from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) has complained about the recommendations made by the commission which inquired into the lobster industry.
My only reference was to the limitation of canneries.

It has been stated that there was a certain combination among the canners along the coast of the maritime provinces in this way: That the number of licenses were limited, and the licenses were in the hands of a few companies, and in that way they could control the industry to a certain extent. It has been a grievance on the coast of the maritime provinces for some time past that the government have refused to grant any more licenses to new canneries, and that in that way they threw the industry into the hands of the people who had previously held licenses. That matter has been investigated by the Fisheries Committee, which has arrived at the conclusion that this policy was not a good policy, and that any person who can qualify himself to carry on a fish cannery in a proper way with the proper equipment should be given a license, and that the so called monopoly should be done away with.
That is exactly what 1 said, only I did not say it as well as the hon. member for Guysboro has said it.

I realize that the minister has bestowed a great deal of time and attention on this subject, but he has not made perfectly clear and plain to me what his position is in respect to certain matters brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Blain) and others. From my limited investigation into such matters, I understand that the injurious effects of a combine may be roughly speaking divided into two classes; in the first place, an undue increase in the price to the consumer; and in the second place, an undue decrease of the price to the persons who produce the raw material, and which the combine works up into the finished article and places on sale. I understand the minister to say that this Bill has relation purely to the operations of the fiTst-class, and that under the Bill as at present framed he did not purpose affording any remedy as Tespects the operations of the second-class. I also understood the minister to state, in a' somewhat indefinite way, that possibly the operations of the second-class may be by some means brought within the scope of this Bill. I ask for information as to that. It seems to me perfectly clear that the operations of those who decrease the price to the purchaser may have no effect whatever on the price to the consumer. It has been suggested that decreasing by means

of a combination, the price to the purchaser, is really an advantage to the whole community as it will inevitably result in decreasing the price to the consumer. 1 do not understand it in that way. It is perfectly possible for la combine to decrease unduly the price to the purchaser and at the same time maintain a reasonable price to consumers, and I have no doubt that has been done.
If it did unduly increase the price to the consumer, would not the Act apply?

You could investigate the matter so far as theTe was an undue increase of price to the consumer, but apparently the producers who are obliged under certain conditions to sell their product for too low a price to that same combine have no opportunity for relief under this Bill.
I wanted to know if this Bill would not cover that?

That is what I want to know also. I understand from the minister that that was not at present within the scope of the Bill, but that after the Bill had been in operation for a year and tested by experience, he might propose to amend it in that direction. Afterwards I understand the minister to intimate, though perhaps not very definitely, that there might be some remedy under the Bill, and I would like to know from him now under what terms of the Bill can operations of the second class to which I have referred be brought within the purview of the Act.

The price is either the result of free competition or the result of some monopolistic factor. If there is absolutely free competition in an article, neither purchaser nor consumer will be affected so far as this measure is concerned-

The minister is not answering my point and perhaps I have nri made myself clear. Take a case where the price charged to the consumer is a perfectly fair and reasonable price and where the consumer has absolutely nothing to complain of. But, although the price charged to the consumer is perfectly fair, there exists a combine by which the price paid to the purchaser of the raw material is unreasonably restricted, so that while the combine itself makes an enormous profit-out of fresh fish for example-the producer of the raw material in the first instance merely obtains the bare cost or perhaps less than the cost of production. Take that case, where the price to the consumer does not come in question at all, is that case covered by this Bill or is it not?

Th!e price is either the result of the play of the law of supply Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
and demand under free competition, or the result of the supply being restricted by some element of a monopolistic nature.
Or the demand being restricted, as in this case.

Any kind of restriction that interferes with the free play of the law of supply and demand in the market may affect the price. Any combination which would b*e sufficiently strong to control the price that could be offered to all producers of a particular article would be a complete monopoly. We cannot imagine such a combination the effect of which would not be reflected in the price the consumers would have to pay for the article. If you have a combination which controls the purchase of all th'e raw material, you have a combination *which stands between the producer and the consumer, not for the benefit of either but, primarily for the benefit of its own. If you have a combination strong enough to keep down the price at which a commodity can be purchased in the open market, it seems to me that you have a prima facie case of a combination standing between the producer and the consumer, and operating to the detriment of the consumer, and therefore coming under the operation of this Act.

I would rather have from the hon. minister a direct answer to my question than a lecture on political economy. I could imagine a case where the price paid to the producer is cut down, while the price charged to the consumer is not increased.
Can the hon. gentleman give such a'case?

I am not called upon to give one, but I could point to an instance of that in the most gigantic trust known in modern times, the Standard Oil Company. My view is that if such a case should arise, the producer whose price is cut down will have no remedy under this Bill. It may be that the hon. minister's great experience of the complexity of human affairs tells him that no such case could arise; but, with all deference to him, I would hardly be inclined to accept his view on that point. We know that in the complexity of modern conditions a great many things do arise *which are not foreseen, and it is not beyond the scope of my limited imagination to realize that there might be a case where the price is kept down to the consumer for the very good reason that the price of the raw material to the producer is also kept down to an unreasonable limit, so that the combination makes a very great profit, while the man who produces the raw mate-

rial makes little or no profit, and works very hard for the barest livelihood.

I may say frankly to my hon. friend that in introducing this legislation the government had not in view the me'eting of every possible evil that might grow out of combinations. The objection which we rather expected to be raised against this measure was that it was going too far. I am very glad to find hon. gentlemen opposite apparently sharing the view that it is a step in the right direction, and that if it has any limitations at all they are that it does not go quite far enough.. I think it meets all the apparent cases which have come to the attention of the government up to the present tim'e. If there are other cases which it * does not cover, time will reveal them, and when it does, I think we can deal with them mor'e to the advantage of the country than we could by making this measure too wide at the outset.

I refrained from making any remarks on this Bill at the beginning of the discussion, though I take considerable interest in it. Perhaps I am not deeply enough versed in political economy to size up the situation fully, but I have some idea of how such matters work out in practice. There are three categories into which trade naturally divides itself: there is first the producer; second, the manufacturer or dealer; and, third, the consumer. Combinations may exist in any of the thre'e categories, and if I wished to delay the House, I could give well-known examples of each class of combination. The hon. member for West-worth (Mr. Sealey), the hon. member for Westminster (Mr. Taylor), spoke truly when they said that this Bill might not cover combinations that would restrict the prices paid to producers. If the minister inserted the word ' producer,' I think he would perhaps make the Bill cover the case exactly. There are combinations of farmers as well as combinations of dealers. For instance, the milk producers and the fruit producers have their little associations by which they endeavour to fix . prices. It seems that the first operation of a combination or trust of this kind is to seek to control the sources of production, because unless a trust can do so it is impossible for ^ to control the price to the consumer. There might be a combination of dealers or drov'ers that would reduce the price of hogs to the farmer, and the farmer under this Bill would have no redress. Three or four drovers might form such a combination among themselves and agree to pay only a certain price for hogs in a certain district. There is nothing in the Bill dealing with a case of that kind.

I admit that there is nothing in the Bill to prevent one or two drovers in a particular locality from fixing the prices they would pay. But if there were half a dozen or more who combined to control a particular area, and the farmers of that area were put in such a position that they could not sell their hogs, except at the price the combination fixed, I think you would have a combination that would be obviously detrimental to the consumer, because it would limit the supply.
Mr; J. A. CURRIE. It might not limit the supply. The sale of bacon and pork in this country is controlled broadly by two firms of retail dealers. They might not care a fig so far as that is concerned, and that is one point in which the Bill is lacking. For example, there is nothing to prevent a combination of^ grain buyers in the west fixing the price of grain in the west irrespective of the foreign market value of it. Everybody knows that the tendency is to form combinations so as to make, prices stable, in order that a man in any line of business will know what profit he is likely to make. If prices fluctuate such as they did in the old oil days-one day a barrel of oil would only be worth 10 cents, and the next day it would be worth $10-these fluctuations would give rise to gamblings and cause great injury to the consumer, and the producer, and everybody else. There is no doubt that combinations have tended to maintain prices at a set level. Suppose the grain dealers form a combination, and fix the price of wheat in the Northwest, what means would the Northwest farmer have to bring about an investigation? I am quite in sympathy with the Bill, but I think the insertion of the word ' producer ' would help out the situation, and make it better for all concerned.

The minister stated that he had made provision under this Bill to deal with all classes of monopoly that have been brought to the attention of the government. I quite understand that the minister is young in the cabinet, but surely he knows that for many years the farming community of the west have come down here delegation after delegation, asking for the passage of legislation which would burst the grain combine. The agricultural organizations in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba have been sending their representatives to Ottawa for years asking the government to deal with that question. They are producers, and if there is no provision under this Bill whereby they can break up that monopoly which they have strong evidence does exist, then the Bill falls very far short of what it should be. Can a combine of that kind be investigated?

Unquestionably, any combination of the kind mentioned by the hon-gentleman could be investigated. If you look at the definition of the word combine, the last sentence says:
And shall include what is known as a trust, monopoly or merger.
All the cases that have been cited affecting producers have been in the nature of monopolies. I think that is admitted. That being so they would come under that definition, and all such cases would be covered by the measure as it stands.

Yes, but the minister has excluded himself from contending that when he accepted the amendment of the hon. member for Pietou which says:
To the detriment of the consumers in such articles of trade and commerce.
The applicant has to show that he is injured as the consumer of the article.

The first part of the definition is limited by the words the hon. gentleman has suggested, but in addition to that there are added the words:
And also includes ' a trust, monopoly and merger/
The word ' also ' is sufficient to show that if these last words are not in the definition itself there can be no doubt the definition was intended to bring them within the measure.

Would it not read:
And also includes what is known as a trust, monopoly or merger, which operates to the detriment of the consumers of such articles of trade and commerce.

Not at all, I would object to adding these words to the last part of
the definition.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

The Minister of Labour. (Mr. King) did not make it very clear to me what effect this interpretation would have. We have combinations in the west in connection with wheat, in connection with beef, in connection with pork. What I would like to know is whether the producer in any of these lines in western Canada could have an investigation under this Bill ?

That certainly was the intention, where the combination would have an effect upon prices. To make it perfectly clear, in view of the discussion that has taken place, I propose to make the definition include producers as -well as consumers. Then there can be no mistake. I would point out to the committee that the discussion really arose on the suggested Mr. STAPLES.	-
amendment of ' combine ' made by the hon. member from Pietou (Mt. Macdonald) whose object, as I understood it, was not to restrict the definition, but to make it clear that the combines affected by this law, must be detrimental to some one. Under the amendment already made, the words added axe ' to the detriment of consumers,' there is a desire that it should be made with equal clearness to apply to producers. My own feeling is that the kind of combinations affected by the law is sufficiently indicated by the final words of this section, ' trust, monopoly or merger,' whether such affect producers or consumers. But I would move that the section be amended so as to read, ' to the detriment of consumers or producers of such article of trade or commerce.'
Is not the point sufficiently covered by the definition contained in the clause as printed?

Some hon. members thought that, possibly, combinations that were not detrimental to any class might be brought under the law by the definition as it' is in the printed Bill. If we add * to the detriment of consumers or producers ' that makes it clear that what we want to reach are only such combinations as are detrimental to some one.

But it says ' fixing the price or rental of any article of trade or commerce, or the cost of the storage or transportation thereof,' and so on. That is the offence, and you limit considerably by the provision concerning its being detrimental to parties.

I would not say that is the offence. The offence lies in a combination of the kind enhancing the price to consumers or lowering them to producers. A combine that does not operate to the detriment of either consumers or producers, what would be the necessity of including it ?	.
But is not what the minister proposes to add-that it is detrimental to some one-implied in the very words of the section?

I think that what the hon. member (Mr. J. Haggart) says as to the definition as printed is quite right. The definition, as printed to#my mind, is sufficient. But some hon. members are inclined to be sensitive as to the words, and wish to make it clear that it is only a combine that is operating detrimentally to others that is to be dealt with by this legislation. The words do not take away anything or add anything, it seems to me. But they do no harm, and they meet the objection raised.

It seems to me the addition of these words does not make a single bit of difference in the working of the Bill. The whole object is to prevent the operation of injurious combines. I do not see any great objection to the words, but I do not see that they add anything to the effect of the Bill.
They are desired by some lion, members of the House.
That is no reason. The minister must be able to give some reasonable explanation.

The reason seems to be quite clear. Some hon. members have desired these words to be inserted because they fear that otherwise the definition may be misread. A man might be afraid to enter into some agreement with his neighbour, fearing that, under this definition, the law would apply to him. By adding the words ' to the detriment of consumers or producers ' you make clear, in the opinion of the hon. members who have spoken, the purpose which it is intended to serve by the definition of ' combine.' If it helps to remove doubts, that is a good reason.

But we are guided by fixed principles. What is meant by ' detrimental to the consumer?' If the judgment is left to the parties appointed under the Act, and no fixed principle is laid down for their guidance, it gives to these parties the power of constituting a crime. There is the objection to legislation of this sort; you make it a crime-[DOT]
No.

Yes, you do. For, if within a certain time after publication in ' the * Canada Gazette,' those whose conduct is investigated, do not cease to do what these parties have held is wrong for them to do, they may be fined $1,000 a day.'
That is after it has been shown that an offence has been committed, namely, that prices have been unduly enhanced; and that, at common law, is crime to-day.
Does the minister say that there are combines in existence that do not reduce the price of the raw material to the producer, or unduly advance the price of the article to the consumer?
There may be such. I would not like to say that any combine does enhance the prices unduly or restrict competition unduly, until I had had a chance of looking into it.

HAGGART I object to any such legislation as this. If we are to have crimes on the statute-book we want to define what the crime is. Under this section,
a party is accused of being guilty of a crime because he detrimentally enhances prices. What does enhancing prices mean? Surely we are entitled to a description or designation of 'enhancing prices,' to know whether we are guilty of a crime or not. But the minister takes the extraordinary position of leaving to a court of arbitration to decide what is meant by enhancing prices. After they come to a decision and publish it in the 'Canada Gazette,' then, after a certain time, it becomes a crime, and you are punished for it. Such a way of designating a crime I never heard of before.

With all due deference, I would like to point out that so far as this legislation puts any class of actions in the category of crimes, my hon. friend will find that in the Criminal Code already, precisely the same thing. If the hon. gentleman will look at section 498 of the Criminal Code, he will find that.
Every one is guilty of an. indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $4,000 and not less than $200, or to two years' imprisonment, or, if a corporation, is liable to a penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars, and not less than one thousand dollars, who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with any other person, or with any railway, steamship, steamboat or transportation company,-
(a)	To unduly limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce; or,
(b)	To restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any such article or commodity ; or,
(c)	To unduly prevent, limit, or lessen the manufacture or production of any such article or commodity, or to unreasonably enhance the price thereof.
If I am not mistaken, the hon. member himself voted for that legislation.
Are you sure of it?
I think so. I think the hon. member supported this legislation when it was introduced by the late Clarke Wallace.
An amendment was introduced to the Criminal Code founded on the Bill that was introduced by Clarke Wallace.
This is the Bill that was introduced by Clarke Wallace.
If I remember rightly, the provisions of that Bill were embodied in the criminal law, and I remember Sir John Thompson saying that it did not alter the law, it made no changes in it.
But did not the hon. gentleman support it?
It made no change in the law, it was a harmless amendment. Is this amendment going to leave the law in the same position it was before?

That is not the point we are discussing. The hon. gentleman is taking exception to my putting on the statutes legislation making a certain set of conditions a crime, when he himself has voted for legislation which does that very thing.

You state that I voted for it, you must have authority for saying so. The possibilities are, as I was a member of the government when it was embodied in the Criminal Code, that I supported it. But I do not suppose there was a vote on the question at all, I suppose it was unanimously adopted by the House. The hon. gentleman has found out that the Act has just the effect that Sir John Thompson said it had, that it did not alter the law in any respect, that it was perfectly harmless, like ia chip in the porridge. The hon. gentleman intends to make the Act something different from what it was before, and that is what I am criticising. The hon. gentleman says it is the same. If it is the same, there is no use in introducing it; if it is different, I have a right to give my opinion on the difference.

It is not the same Bill. The first time the Act passed this House it did not contain the words ' unduly ' or ' unreasonably.' Those words were put in by the Senate, and when the Bill came back here, because of the lateness of the session, and because we knew that the Bill must drop entirely if this House did not accept the amendment made by the Senate, we accepted it. But afterwards, in 1899, I moved an amendment to strike those words out and did get them struck out in this House. The Bill then went to the Senate, and they introduced them again. The following year I introduced the Bill again, and got it through this House, and through the Senate, without those words ' unduly ' or ' unreasonably '. But the following year it was amended by the present government, those words were put back again, and I believe now, and always did believe that it was amended for that specific purpose, because when the original Bill was on the statutes, and it was submitted to Sir .Oliver Mowat, who, as Attorney General of Ontario, would be obliged to enforce the law, he said it was utterly useless, that no person could go before a court, and get a court to say what was ' unduly ' or ' unreasonably ' enhancing prices; but if these words were left out, then the Bill would be useful. The very next year the government amended the Criminal Code, and put these words back again, and I always believed that they put them back so as to make the Bill practically worthless.

I want to say now that I am in favour of this legislation, if it will have the effect aimed at. There is a suspicion in our country that there is a restraint of trade to the extent that the farmers generally do not get full value for what they produce, and also that they pay more than they should pay, in many cases for what they consume. I hope the Bill is right, but as I am not a lawyer, I am not able to judge of the effect of certain sections.

I want to say a word upon this amendment. I understood that the minister's object was to benefit the consumer. But my opinion is that when the minister has amended the interpreta-i tion clause by including the word ' producer,' he entirely neutralizes the benefit of the Act to the consumer. If you have a combine, or a monopoly that increases the cost to the consumer by an investigation under this Act, you are not likely to benefit the producer. The one is adverse to the other. The producer of a certain article that is sold under a monopoly, shares in the benefit of that monopoly. In my opinion this section is decidedly better as 'it is. The object of the Bill is to benefit the consumer, and to the extent that you are benefiting the consumer by destroying monopoly you cannot at the same time benefit a particular producer who produces the article in question. You are very likely to reduce the return he gets from the production of that article. I certainly think that the interpretation section would be better without the word ' producer You do not help the consumer by trying to benefit the producer at the same time.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5, order for investigation.
Would you not amend this to conform to the amendments made before?

Yes, the words ' or producer,' should be added after the words ' consumers,' where they appear in lines 24, 34 and 44. I therefore, beg to move:
That the words ' or producers ' be inserted after the word ' consumers ' in lines 24, 35 and 45.
Amendment agreed to.
I propose that the section be amended by adding, after the word ' persons,' in the first line the words ' British subjects resident in Canada, and of full age.'
Amendment agreed to.
I also propose that after the word ' that ' in line 42 paragraph 4, there be inserted the words ' the alleged combine operates to the detriment of the declarant as a consumer or producer.'

What would be the effect if an application were received under that section, and an investigation took place, and if three of the six were trying to prove that the producer was affected, and the other three were trying to prove that the consumer was affected?
_ Mr. KING. I think if they succeeded in proving that, there would he a double reason for going (ahead.

What is the meaning of the phrase ' injurious to trade? ' There have been a great many decisions defining the meaning of the phrase ' in restraint of trade.' A great many things are decided to be in restraint of trade, and there are a great many decisions as to what the expression means. But perhaps the meaning that the minister wishes to convey is a little different.
I think the meaning is clear.
Would you not under this Bill attack labour unions as well as combinations?

When I moved the second reading of the measure I stated that it was my intention to move in committee to add a clause to make it quite clear that this measure would not take away from trades organizations the rights secured to them under the existing law. I intend to move an amendment to this effect before the committee rise3.

It seems to me that the point taken by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is worthy of consideration. The phrase ' injurious to trade,' is a novel one in legislation of this character. I do not think it has been defined at all. I do not recollect 'any definition of any such phrase in decisions regarding legislation of this kind. I think that if the words ' in restraint of trade,' were used you would be going along a path where you had well recognized conditions, and where the bodies having to do with the operation of this statute would understand clearly where they were working, and with quite as good results. I think that the suggestion of the hon. member for North Simcoe as to what the word ' injurious ' means is very pertinent to the discussion. What it does mean, from a legal standpoint, in working out this Bill, is something that I do not think anybody could venture a very strong opinion on with a view of arriving at exactitude with reference to it; whereas, the words * in restraint of trade,' have had a usage, and definition for centuries. Their significance is well _ understood. I think that the language is more apt apart from the legal standpoint.

The idea of the minister is to express the same thing, and
that is why I thought that using the old word would make it more clear instead of having the courts give a definition of what injurious ' is. The courts have decided hundreds of times what ' restraint of trade ' is.

In my opinion the words are quite plain, and I think they had better be left as they are.
On section II-members of board.

You have here the words:	'Being one of the parties to the
investigation.' Would that be taken to mean that the party to be appointed should be one of the persons who had applied?	1

There can only be two parties to the investigation, the party complaining and the party complained against.
ivir. j. a. (JUKKIE. These words were evidently inserted parenthetically to make it clear what the effect is. They would seem to infer that one of the parties who should be on the board would be one of the applicants, while it was evidently the intention of the minister that the parties who asked for the investigation and the parties who were named in the complaint should each select a representative.
What would the hon. gentleman suggest?

This drafting in the Bill is according to the usual phraseology, but I should prefer that the statement should be more direct, so that nobody could mistake it. Why not say: The . parties who have applied for this investigation shall name one of the members of the board; the parties complained against shall name another member, and these two members of the board shall appoint a third?

I do not know much about the^ legal effect of this language, but I think I know what words mean, and I do not see how any words could make it more clear than those used in the Bill. It states that one member of the board shall be appointed on the recommendation of the persons on whose application the order is granted.
Read on.
Then it says: Being one of the parties to the investigation. Well, I do not see why these words should be there at all.

If these words obscure the meaning w'e can strike them out. I am quite agreeable to have that done.
(The words ' being one of the parties- to the investigation ' were stricken from the Bill.)

On section 13,
No person shall act as a member of the board who has any direct pecuniary interest in the alleged combine that is the subject of investigation by such board, or who is not a British subject.

It seems to me that no person should be a member of the board who is one of the applicants for the investigation. If there is to be a public advantage derived from the Bill, it will be only had if the board is absolutely impartial and unprejudiced, as far as that is possible. I would like to suggest to the minister the advisability of inserting after the word ' who ' in the first line the words ' is one of the applicants for the board.'
I will be very glad to accept the suggestion of the hon. membeT for Pictou.

I would also suggest after the woTd ' direct ' the addition of the words ' or indirect.' I may say that I am very much disappointed that the hon. Minister of Labour has not the Minister of Justice sitting beside him while this Bill is being considered. It is a very important measure, liable to affect the interests of a great many people, we are all trying to make it as perfect as possible, arid 1 think it is a matter worthy of comment that the Minister of Justice is not in his place in the House to assist the Minister of Labour in the phraseology of the Bill, because he will be concerned to a large extent in carrying it out.
I may say that the Minister of Justice has already gone over the Bill, as it was drafted by the Department of Justice.

It seems to me that we are all indirectly interested in these investigations, and consequently the insertion of the words ' or indirectly ' would defeat the whole object of the Bill.
Amendment suggested by Mr. E. M. Macdonald agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 15-oath of office-

It seems to me that this section should be amended to provide that the members of the board shall make an affidavit negativing any interest in the application or the result of the investigation. Otherwise you might have the parties who have applied for an investigation choosing as their representative on the board, somebody who is as much interested in the application or in the result of the investigation as they are. The result of the working out of this Act can only be ascertained by having it worked out by a board that is absolutely impartial and that has no interest in the result of the investigation.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is hardly possible, because the one thing provided for is the interest of the whole public in the result of the investigation.
I think the point raised is covered by the first clause of the oath: ' I will truly, faithfully and impartially perform my duties as a member of the board.'

I am afraid the minister's logic is hardly good enough in regard to that, because if so we should omit the third clause as to whether they are interested pecuniarily. Language like this might be used, and I think it is only fair that it should be used, that the investigating member should be prepared to make an affidavit that ' I am not injuriously or otherwise affected by the alleged combine.'
If it is a combine adversely affecting the public, he could not take such an affidavit.
I think I could show you readily how he could. In the first place, combines that form the subject of investigation are not merely combines that have ramifications all over the Dominion of Canada.
They might have.

They might have, but at the same time if they might have, there is just as much room for saying that there are numbers of people who are not directly pecuniarily affected. Cases in which you have combinations with wide ramifications are very few. The majority of instances in which this Act will have to be applied will be cases affecting particular localities. Thus in western Ontario you might have combinations there that injuriously affect certain consumers in that locality. Well, there is no reason why you should be compelled to accept as one of the investigators some one who lives in that locality and who would be undoubtedly chosen by the parties making the application, because they would think he was in sympathy with them. But go to the central portion of Ontario, and you would get a man absolutely independent and who would not be affected by the results in any way whatever. It seems to me that this business of having investigating boards composed of men who are interested in the result is only going to have consequences that will have no value to us. That a party who is going to act as judge should not be in a position to say that he is entirely disinterested would be an anomalous position of affairs, and I do think that any man who sits on a board of this kind ought to be so disinterested that he should be able to say he is or is not in-* juriously or otherwise affected by the alleged combine.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
With all deference to my hon. friend, I do not agree with him. He

is endeavouring to make fish of one and flesh of another. There may be combines that only affect certain individuals. Ori the other hand, there may be combines that affect the country generally. Now, you cannot possibly have a man take an affidavit in one case and not in another. We must make the whole Act apply in a general way, otherwise the Act will be absolutely nullified. Even supposing you were to endeavour to do something in that way in the case of smaller combines which do not affect every person, I do not see how a man in that case could take it, becausa there can be no question about it that any great production in respect to which an inquiry is asked by reason of an alleged' combine, must in some way or other direct-# ly or indirectly affect the applicants. I cannot possibly see how you could do that. In passing legislation of this kind, you must have simply a general oath such as this and let it work out the best way. I cannot see any other way possible.

We provide as well that the parties who sign the application should make a declaration. That affects themselves, and if it affects themselves to any extent, they must have some pecuniary interest in it.
Mr.	McLEAN. (Suppose it is a sugar
combine, every man in the country would be interested in that, every person who uses sugar would be. Or suppose we had a grocers' combine, as we were supposed to have a short time ago, everybody in the country is interested pecuniary in that. Consequently the contention of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) is hardly sound.

I think the common, ordinary criminal procedure is that a juryman has to take a pretty stiff oath. In several countries the man who enters the jury box to decide between a criminal and the law has virtually to swear that he knows nothing about the case that he has heard nothing about the case that he is not interested in it, and that he has not made up his mind on it one way or the other. There is no doubt that this Act partakes of a similar character. I think the sentence proposed is: 'I am not miuriously affected', but a man could be affected without being injuriously affected. For instance a man might be affected by a sugar combine, but he might be a rich man, and it would not matter to him perhaps five cents a year.
It would affect him all the same.

There is no doubt that this law as it stands is going to make criminal prosecutions, and these arbitrators will stand in the same position as jurymen at an ordinary inquest. 13 do not 251
see why they should not be compelled to take the same oath, so as to prevent any miscarriage of justice one way or the other. I think it is the only fair way, and I 'think the minister should consider the redrafting of this declaration so as to cover all the points raised. It would be very unfair for a man to take an oath that he is not. interested in the combine, when he might be a purchaser from that combine and therefore very strongly interested in soaking the combine. There are two sides to it, and I think we should meet the case thoroughly.
. Mr. BLAIN. This Bill, I understand, from the hon. minister has been submitted to the Justice Department, and has been the subject of consideration on the part of the present _ government for a great many months, if not years. The government, as the minister has pointed out, has been aware and is still aware of combines existing in this 'country, that at least affect the consumer, and I have no doubt, particularly in the west the beef combine affects the producer as well. I do not know that it is important that all those details should be looked into. I believe the minister and the department should take the full responsibility. After a year goes by, we will expect that the minister will be able to come forward and state to this House and to the country that these great evils have been driven out by this legislation. I hope we will not be disappointed. If we are, the minister will have to answer to parliament and to the country for the disappointment. It seems to me the government after giving this careful consideration has presented this perfected Bill. Whether it is perfect or not I cannot say. I do not know whether the minister himself would say that it is'a perfect Bill. It was rather suggested that after a year had passed by it would be found that some people in Canada had not been reached by this Bill and that there might foe an opportunity to amend it. I have my own opinion as to whether it will be effective legislation or not, but it is not my business to say whether it is or is not. I think the minister having taken the full responsibility, having by the introduction of this Bill told the people of Canada that there are evils in the shape of combines affecting the country generally, the producer and the consumer in some cases. I think the minister should take the full responsibility. For myself, I am willing to leave it on the shoulders of the minister and on the shoulders of the government. Thev have been thirteen or fourteen vears looking this matter up, and the delays have greatly disappointed the people of Canada. These gentlemen, before they came into power, talked of combinations, particularly my good friend the Minister of



Customs (Mr. Paterson). He saw combines everywhere when he was in opposition, but he has sat quietly by while in government and has 'contented himself with spending enormous amounts of money. Now, after all these years have passed, he comes forward, with his new friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), and 'proposes legislation 1 to check the evils that have been going on all this time. I think we ought to give these lion, gentlemen an opportunity to deal with these questions, and, for my part, I propose to give them that opportunity. After a year goes by, we may have something to say as to their legislation, and the way it has been carried out.

My suggestion is that no person should act on the board who is prejudiced. Those who are prejudiced should be barred as much as those who are interested. I have not thought out the wording, but some words should be added to cover that idea.

Every man of the board must swear that he will perform his duties 'truly, faithfully and impartially.' If he cannot be bound by an oath of that kind. I do not know that any form of words will help particularly.

I feel very strongly with regard to this matter. No tribunal should be constituted by tnis or any other legislature, the effect of whose decision is to fix criminal liability upon individuals unless the impartiality of the tribunal by whom the facts are to be investigated is ensured. To that proposition, I think, no one will raise objection. Under the Act, as it stands, you prevent any person who initiates the proceedings from being a member of the board. At the same time there is no reason why you should not have the partner of one of these applicants sitting as a member of the board and deciding the result. The business competitors of a man might initiate these procedings and then have a friendly business associate interested in the same matter, sitting on the board and using all the powers given by the Act to secure information, not for the benefit of the public, but to gratify some feeling or benefit a competitor in the business.
