Does not my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald), who is making valuable suggestions, believe that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Justice have considered all these matters?

I am one of those who do not yield my judgment and conscience to the Minister of Labour, or the Minister of Justice, or anybody else. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) may be prepared to do that in the case of the leaders of his party, but I am not. I hold Mr BLAIN.
myself free to discuss freely any matter that comes before this House. And I have, an opinion of my own in legal matters which I do not yield to anybody, while I respect the opinion of others. My contention is that there should be a clause providing that those who sit on this board shall not be interested in the application, connected with the trade or business directly affected by the application. Under the Conciliation Act, we have had cases where it has brought about a very satisfactory result, and where its intent and theory have been worked out. But we have had other cases where members of the board have had their opinion absolutely fixed and settled before the investigation was begun, should be constituted by this or any result. Why should we give a black eye to this Bill at its very inception by permitting parties who are directly interested in the business directly affected, to sit in judgment on these matters? There should be as complete a guarantee as possible of impartiality in these important matters.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Suppose an application were made by six farmers relating to a matter of which the Grange and farmers associations had made a particular study, and one that affects their industry, would my hon friend (Mr. Macdonald) provide that no farmer should be a member of the boards to investigate the matter? Every farmer would be interested to some slight degree in the business directly affected. To make such a provision would be to nullify the whole Act.

I can suppose a great many cases in which you would have a board which -would include persons directly interested in learning the business of the parties charged with forming a combine. The prosecution might be a mere effort to wreak vengeance or spite or to obtain business secrets, and not an effort for the good of the country. If the case my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) speaks of arose in Lambton, the farmers of that county, who have been accustomed_ to look to my hon. friend to guard their interests in legal matters, could well ask to have him as their representative on the board, and he would do the work as well as one of themselves,

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I would be getting votes, and so would be directly interested.

No, I am sure my hon. friend would not do that. All I contend is that the Bill should be so amended as to cover the principle that interested parties shall not be members of the board so that the impartiality of the board should be assured.

Those against whom the charge is made under this Bill might well prefer that some person having knowledge

of the business should be a member of the board. Suppose that a certain line of manufacture is alleged to be under a combine. The people concerned would feel it decidedly in their interest to have a manufacturer on the board who would understand the conditions of their business. It seems to me that the provision of the Bill that no person shall act as a member of the board who has a direct pecuniary interest in the alleged combine is as far as we ought to go.

It is quite correct to say that there is nobody so capable of judging these matters as one who has some knowledge of the business affected, but, as I understand the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) he seeks to prevent the rivals of a business concern from using this law to pry into the affairs of that concern. It would be very easy to get six men to swear out affidavits and start an investigation for the very purpose of prying into a rival's business.
A man of that sort would have a pecuniary interest in the combine -he would be interested in getting hold of the business of the combine-and, as such, he could not swear that he was not interested.

I do not- see how it would be possible to carry out the suggestion of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). I think the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) put the case correctly. [DOT] For instance, suppose that six farmers in the west believe that there is a combine among the grain buyers to keep down the price of wheat, and they apply for an investigation. When those six have made application it seems to me the suggestion of the member for Pictou would prevent any farmer in the west from being on the board of arbitration. I do not see how it would be possible to carry out the suggestion of my learned friend, who certainly understands the law better than I do. But looking at it in that practical way, there would have to be some farmer on that arbitration board in order that there may not be any increase in the price of wheat.

Will the minister be good enough to let that clause stand till we can consider it more fully?
On section 20, publication of reports.

I do not wish to oppose this Bill in any way, but sinpe three members are provided for on this commission, why should there be a minority report? What effect will a minority report have? If a certain trade or interest is represented, then this confirms the idea of the member for Pictou, that there is some one person on the board to represent a cer-
251J
tain specific interest, and when the other two have decided what is to be done, the third shall have the privilege of filing in any kind of report he wishes. I hold there should be only one report. You put a prejudiced man on this board, and he will send in a minority report that may be untruthful, and very damaging to the party investigated, and that minority report is given just as much currency as" the majority report. I would ask the minister to consider whether it would not be better to take that clause out.

The reason for permitting a minority report is precisely the same "as the reason for permitting a dissenting judgment where you have several judges sitting on a case. When one judge dissents from the other, it is customary to give the same publicity to his dissenting judgment as to the judgment of the majority of the court.

There are some members in this House who do not hold that there should be any minority judgment. I think there should be only one judgment, and we would have far fewer appeals if only one judgment were published.
On section 21, reduction of customs duties to secure reasonable competition.
Is there not legislation of this kind already?

This section is already on the statutes., with the difference that the present section includes the finding of the board. This section should be read along with section 47 which repeals section 12 of the Customs Act.
On section 22, revocation of patent in certain cases.
That is in the Patent Act also, is it not?

No. The Patent Act relates to the selling of the patented article at a reasonable price, but it does not cover the cases of persons holding a patented article, and, before selling it, requiring the purchaser to enter into an agreement to purchase other things as well from the patent owner, and from him to the exclusion of ail others. This section is intended to prevent cases of that kind.

The use of a patented article is unduly to enhance or lessen competition. Supposing a patented article is used in another article that is beinsr manufactured, the effect of it is to lessen competition, or increase the price to a larger extent than the value of the patent itself.

The law specially refers to that particular form of monopoly and doe; so for reasons of public policy, and to

that extent patents are perhaps more favoured by the general law with reference to enhancing prices than they otherwise would be.

The general law affects them, but I think the effect of this clause is to alter the general law to the extent that it gives jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court, on the recommendation of this board, to cancel a patent.

As I think I pointed out, the present law in regard to patents sets forth the conditions on which a patented article can be sold as to the matter of price. Section 22 does not affect the existing law in that particular in one way or the other. What it relates to is the seller of a patented article making use of the patent to enforce upon persons desiring to use (the patented articlei some contract which limits his power to purchase articles elsewhere than from the patentee himself. That is a different thing altogether.

May I be permitted to ask a question with respect to that clause of the Customs law that allows the government to reduce or strike off the duty if it finds that a combine exists in Canada which is unduly enhancing the pric'e to the consumer? Has that clause been applied against any combine other than the news print paper combine?
As I understand that is the only case that has been investigated.
How long has it been on the statute-book?
I think the Act was passed in 1897, but apparently there have not been many representations to the government as to the necessity for conducting investigations under that section.

This has been on the statute-book since 1897, and there has only been one case. If the government were aware that combines existed in Canada to unduly enhance the price of articles, and if they were empowered to strike off or reduce th'e duty, one would think that, if there were a necessity for legislation of this kind, the government would have put into operation the legislation that they have on the statute-book at th'e present time.

The government would hardly be justified in removing duties or commencing investigations unless very full representations were made in the first instance, as to the need of such investigation, and I understand that such representations have not been made under the law as it stands at the present time. One of the reasons given, I believe, in certain quarters, is that the fear of expense in the matter of an inquiry under the existing law has det'er-Mr. KING.
red many persons who believe that combines were existing, from putting in any representations under that section. This measure is doing away with the cost on the part of consumers who ask for an inquiry.

I would hav'e thought that a department, such as that upon which my hon. friend has been spending a large amount of money, which has been gathering information of this kind, and which has taken the opportunity from time to time of impressing upon the Canadian people that there are combines in Canada that are unduly enhancing prices to the consumer, would have suggested that it would be a good thing to put into force some of the legislation the government have rather than introduce further legislation.

I may say that this legislation is in part the result of investigations which have been made by the Department of Labour. I mentioned these investigations on the second reading of the Bill, investigations which go to show that the cost of living has very materially increased the last few years and which have pointed directly to the need of such legislation as this.

This clause, I understand, covers the case of shoe machinery largely. It is intended, I take it, to meet the United Shoe Machinery Company's case. They are manufacturers of a complete line of machinery, but they will not sell; they will simply lease. There are other manufacturers of shoe ' machinery, but they do not make a full line, and if you want to make shoes, you have to get the United Shoe Machinery Company's full line or otherwise you cannot get a complete line at all. This clause will meet such a case, will it not?

Yes, it is hoped that this section will meet possible combinations of that sort.
On section 23, combines _ restricting manufacture, trade or competition.
If you cannot go before a court and establish the meaning of the words ' unduly and unreasonably,' how are you going to do it before this board?

The board will have opportunities of getting very full information from a variety of sources and of making comparisons. I would think that the board will not have much difficulty in making up its mind as to the meaning of the word ' unreasonably.'

So have the courts such opportunities. Each side will take good care that all information that will sustain one side or the other will be brought before the court. If the court cannot decide what the word * unduly ' means-and this

board becomes in reality a court for the time being-I do not understand how thisi board is going to do it.
The courts have in some cases decided that the enhancement has been unreasonable and undue.
I do not remember any case.
There was the Brantford coal combine case, and there was also the case of the lumber combine at Edmonton.
There was a prosecution?
Yes, a prosecution in which the parties were convicted of an undue enhancement of the price.

Was not that very trouble the cause of the failure in a grocer's case? There was one case entered at Brantford; it is a good while since, but my memory of it is that it was dropped because of the impossibility of successfully proving that prices were unduly enhanced.

As I remember the judgment in the grocer's case, it did not relate to the question of undue or unreasonable enhancement. It found rather that the Grocers' Guild was not a combination in restraint of trade at all. The question of the undue enhancement or unreasonableness of the price was not mentioned in the judgment.
What are you going to do in this trial? What will be necessary in order to convict a person upon such a trial?
If a person is found guilty ' of unduly limiting the facilities for transportation, producing, manufacturing, sup-lying, storing, or

I know what the words of the Bill are; I can Tead them, but I was asking whether the whole investigation will have to be gone through with again, or whether you will put in the proceedings of the board and convict the person in question upon the report of the board.

As to criminal proceedings, I should think it would be necessary to prove the parties guilty under the criminal law and to give them all the rights in the matter of protection which criminal procedure would secure to them. The procedure before the board is not necessarily the procedure to be adopted in a criminal court, and much evidence may be admitted in the general investigation before the board which would not be admitted in a criminal court. For that reason, I think the parties before they are convicted criminally should receive such protection as the criminal procedure and rules of evidence afford.

Then, according to what the minister says, when a party is interested in the criminal court it will be necessary to make out a case against him exactly as if there had been no investigation before the board.

With this difference between that situation and the law as it stands at the present time, that the evidence already before the board would be available. It could not be submitted of course as prima facie evidence, but the facts gathered in that way could be used before the criminal court.
Does the minister mean that the evidence taken before the board could be put in as evidence under the indictment?
No, but the examination before the board would reveal certain facts which any one would be at liberty to use.
The minister means that the evidence would be a soTt of brief in the hands of the prosecuting counsel.
It might serve as that.
That is the extent to which it would be useful?

At present it is plain that the Criminal Code is really of little value in these cases, because of the difficulty of obtaining data upon which to proceed. These examining boards would disclose the fact whether there was a combination or not that should. be proceeded against under the Criminal Code. .

I thought at first that the Bill was a sort of guillotine, and that when the party accused had passed through the investigating board he would have his toilet made and his boots cleaned ready for the criminal court to award the punishment. It seems now that all this investigation before the board amounts to nothing and that if you are to punish the party found guilty you must have a retrial in the criminal court.

The hon. gentleman allows nothing for the effect of publicity and the influence which public opinion is likely to have. If the result of the investigation was a report that a combination existed injurious to trade and harmful to the consumer there would be very strong reason to suspect that that combination if it were to continue a course of conduct reported as detrimental to the public would be proceeded against criminally.

If public opinion has anything to do with this Bill it will have a very poor opinion of it. I fancy that a prosecution launched in this way would run on for generations like the celebrated [DOT] case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

The minister evidently does not know his own Bill. It says: ' any person reported by this board to have been guilty,' etc.-then on line 40: 'is guilty of an indictable offence and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding $1,000,' etc. I take it that after the board has found a man guilty of an indictable offence all you have to do is to take him before a judge to have him sentenced. If the evidence says he is found guilty of an indictable offence, why, the jury would not leave the box; they would say: Yes, he has been tried and found guilty of an indictable offence. Can a man be indicted twice for the same offence?

It says that he must
continue to offend.
It does not, I understand the English language as well as the hon. member.

I don't profess to know very much about the English language, but I think that is the meaning of the
clause.
He may be found guilty of the offence by the board, but he does not become liable to any penalty unless he continues to so offend.
I cannot see it that way. I think you had better amend the Bill so as to make this one Act do the whole business instead of holding a doublebarrelled shot gun over everybody.
I think the meaning of it perhaps is that you have to prove that he was guilty at some time in the past and that he is also guilty at the present time. You have to prove that he is guilty twice.

You certainly would have to prove that he continued to offend. If after the 'boaTd reported the conditions changed, as probably in nine case out of ten they would, through the force of public opinion, there would be no necessity for seeking to recover a penalty. If the party continued to offend he would be liable to a penalty. "
If public opinion does not get in its work then it is necessary to show that he has been guilty at some particular period in the past and that he has continued and is guilty at the present time.
If the board finds he has been guilty, how aTe you going to determine that he has continued to offend?
At that point the criminal law comes into play and he becomes criminally liable and would be proceeded acainst in the criminal courts in the regular manner.

The question is: what is the real effect of the finding of the board so far as the crime is concerned? Apparently the first element of the proof, once the criminal proceeding was initiated, would be to prove that there was a report of the board that the person had been guilty of these different offences, or some one of them, and with that report counsel trying the case would take the first step. Is that report prima facie evidence of the fact that the party has been guilty or has it any value whatever except as being just an elementary proposition in the course of the case. The fact that the report has been made may be evidence of the guilt of the party accused so far as the past transaction is concerned, or it may not. It may be that the absence of the words: ' such report shall be prima facie evidence of the fact that a combination had existed at a certain time,' renders it necessary for the prosecutor to go all through the thing again and to show the facts which the board deemed sufficient to found the report upon. If the report is to have the effect and it is to be of itself evidence of a combination having existed at a certain time, then there ought to be some procedure by which that report can be set aside if it was erroneous, so that the party found guilty could get to an appellate tribunal. It may be that certiorari would apply. If it does not, there ought to be an appeal from the decision of the board. It seems to me jt ought to be made fairly clear what the value of that report is. The finding of a tribunal constituted as this tribunal is, ought not to be taken as absolute or conclusive proof of the guilt of anybody without the party having the right to appeal from it. I am aware that this clause is open to the construction that a party prosecuting would need to show three things: first, the fact that a report had been made; secondly, that over and above the report, the accused was guilty of combining to the detriment of consumers or producers as the case may be, within the meaning of the Act; thirdly, that after the report of the board finding him guilty of combining to the detriment of consumers, he still continues to offend. If a certificate of the report is to be taken as ample evidence to warrant the conviction of the accused, it ought to be open to the parties to have an appeal, or to have the report reviewed even before it forms prima facie evidence against them in a criminal proceding.

The view of the Minister of Justice on this section is that if the parties were indicted criminally it would be necessary to prove their guilt in the regular manner. The evidence taken before one of these boards would undoubtedly be of service to the prosecuting counsel in the case, but the report itself would not be prima

facie evidence. The guilt of the parties would have to be proven in the regular way, allowing them the benefits of such procedure as the criminal law provides.

The hon. member for Pietou must observe that the hon. minister intends to make the procedure as simple as possible, and not to play into the hands of legal gentlemen in Nova Scotia or elsewhere, and thus burden the affair with costs.

My hon. friend from Lanark will agree with me in one thing, that the gentlemen accused of combinations will have to come to the legal profession to get the affair properly worked out. I take it that the opinion of the Minister of Justice, as given us by the hon. Minister of Labour, is practically this, that the production of the certificate of the report of the board before the court dealing with the criminal charge is only evidence of the fact that the report was made, and that it is necessary for the prosecutor to show, entirely apart from the report, that the accused is guilty of a criminal combination against the Act, and that he continues to offend.
Yes, that Is the opinion of the Minister of Justice.

I would like the minister to consider the advisability of inserting in this section an amendment which would give the parties charged the same right that is now given under section 498 of the Criminal Code to parties charged with unduly limiting competition or unreasonably increasing the price. They have a right after the preliminary investigation to have their case determined by a judge of a Superior Court or a judge of the Supreme Court, as the case may be, without a jury. It seems to me that this principle applied in the Criminal Code to a case of a much greater offence ought to be applied to this case.

That point has been raised in one or two communications that I have received, and it has been considered. The hon. member will notice that in the proceedings under the Criminal Code there had not been any prior investigation, any finding against the parties, and they have not had an opportunity of changing their course of conduct before any further action is taken. In view of the fact that the parties are specially protected in that way, and that they are given ten days in which to change their course of conduct which is deemed detrimental to the public interest, the necessity of taking the precaution which the hon. gentleman has suggested is removed.

Let us see how that will work out. It is presumed that public
opinion is against everything in the nature of combines. Proceedings have been initiated, and a case has got to the final trial before a judge and jury. The prosecutor may show that evidence taken before the investigation established tne fact that at some time there was a combination which is an offence against this Act. Suppose he goes along so far, and he has very little evidence. In fact the weight of evidence may be the other way; he may have very little evidence that the accused has continued to offend. Now there might be some evidence with which to go to a jury, and the result would be that recognizing the existence of this public opinion, though the parties had if not absolutely, the weight of evidence in their favour to show that they had ceased to offend, that conviction would be had against them, 'whereas I do not think that it would be had so readily if you had a judge to weigh the evidence. I do not think that men engaged in business, and committing those novel crimes that my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), thinks are so peculiar, should be treated so arbitrarily. It seems to me that the question of determining whether or not there has been a continuation of the offence, should be determined by a judge, because it is a matter of weighing evidence which a judge can do far better than a jury. In that way I think it is extending this legislation to an unwarrantable extent to take away from the parties in business who happen to have an arrangement, but who have ceased operating under it, those rights now accorded to them under the Criminal Code.

If those proceedings are to be worth anything at all they must be as simple as possible. What does my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) intend to do? There is an investigation in the first place by a judge as to whether there is a prima facie case or not; then there is a referendum to this board of arbitration to find out whether the prices have been unduly enhanced or not, and still before this finding can take any effect it is suggested that the party have a right to an investigation or a retrial be-for a judge. A case of this kind would put the celebrated Jarndyce into oblivion in the number of courts and appeals and trials for the purpose of finding out whether a party is guilty of unduly enhancing prices or not. Now, in the interests I represent, the farming interests, what is wanted is simplicity in our legislation. One beauty of this court is that it is not going to cost the litigants anything; the country is to pay the costs. That may be something of an argument in favour of the proposition of the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) but on the general principle I think we ought to limit

the appeals from the different courts. We are legislating in the interests of the country, and as we are paying the expenses of all this inquiry it should be as short as possible. I am in favour of the minister's principle, that instead of lengthening those inquiries they should be shortened as much as possible.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: There is one thing I would like to suggest. It might be that ten days would be rather a short time to enable some of those concerns to so rearrange matters as to come within the order of the board. I would make the suggestion to the committee that perhaps after the word 'day' you might add these words, or words with the same meaning: ' Or such further extension of time as in the opinion of the board may be necessary'. I think it should be in the option of the board to make a longer period if they think fit.
What line would that be in?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: In the forty-third line after the word 'day'.
What penalty is now imposed under the Criminal Code for a combine?
Not exceeding $4,000 and not less than $200, or two years imprisonment. In the case of a corporation it is not exceeding $10,000, and not less than $1,000.
Is it intended that these penalties should be cumulative, that you shall also impose that $10,000 in addition to the penalty in the Act?
For each day that they continue.
If they are found guilty of continuing then the penalty under the Code would not only be exacted, but the penalty under this Act as well; otherwise this clause is meaningless.
The parties would state, I presume, under which section they were bringing their action, and if they brought their action under this section, the penalties provided here would be applicable.

But the minister said there is no provision exacting any penalty unless there is a continuation of the offence, and in order to insure that you will have to have recourse to the Criminal God.e. In that case would the party be liable to the penalties under the Criminal Code only, or also to the penalties in this Act?
This clause would constitute an addition to the Criminal law. You are making a new offence here which becomes part of the Criminal law.

I believe with the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) that in legislation of this kind we should have simplicity. As I understand it, after a man has gone through this investigation, and has been found guilty, it does not end with his ceasing to be a party to a combine. Any person, those who originally entered the prosecution against him, could turn round and indict him for a previous offence, and indict him under the Code. Or does this legislation block any indictment under the Code?
Certainly not.
Then this is a double barrelled gun?
Why should it not be?

I think the minister should simply add some clause that when parties are found guilty of combining under this section, the board should inflict a fine not exceeding a certain amount of money, and let it go at that. Then if the party continued for a certain length of time, he could be indicted under the Code. I think that would be the sensible way. As it is it subjects the parties to three distinct separate and parallel prosecutions for the same Act.

The general opinion to-day in regard to combines that violate the law is that the present penalties are not severe or numerous enough. I am glad that my hon. friends think that this legislation is making the penalties more severe and adding to the number, because some other hon. members on the same side rather indicated that this law did not go far enough.
Does this section cover the case of a combine which has resulted in unduly increasing the price to the producer?

The hon. member was not in the House, I think, when I added to the definition of the word ' combine ' the. words ' or producer ' in order to meet what I think was the wish of the hon. member, and other members of the House, that it should be made quite clear the law would be applicable to that kind of a case.

I think I was in the House then, but the particular offences within the scope of this section seemed to be set out here in distinct terms, and not by a reference to the interpretation clause. Therefore, the interpretation clause, even although it has been amended by the hon. minister, does not seem to be of very much assistance in that regard.
Possibly I can explain how the difficulty arose. The clause as originally drafted did not contain
I understand that. I am not talking about that, but about this section. Is th'ere any reference here to the interpretation clause? Perhaps I have overlooked that.
This section, as it stands, is broad enough to cover any kind of an agreement in restraint of trade. It would include restraint against producers as well as against consumers.

It struck m'e that it did not cover the case of fixing prices which were not enhanced. For example, the millers might say:	We will give the
farm'ers 70 cents a bushel for their wheat this season. That would be fixing the price, and, according to the interpretation clause as I understand it, it would be against the law. But it would not be enhancing the price, and this section provides, as to prices, only against unreasonably enhancing them.
It provides against * unduly restraining or injuring trade or commerce in relation to any such article.' That covers the fixing of prices if fixing has that effect.

I think the minister has not understood my question. I understand him to say that under this section there is no liability to a fine unless the party has been found guilty by the board and subsequently convicted "under the Criminal Code.

I do not know what I could have said to convey that impression. Parties are liable, if found guilty under this section, and if they continue to offend, to a penalty not exceeding $1,000 a day and costs. The Criminal Code stands as at present._ As soon as th'ere has been an investigation into an alleged combine and a board has reported that a combine exists, parties may, if they wish, proceed under this section to recover the penalty of so much a day for the length of time the combine continues to operate in a way detrimental to the public, or they may take proceedings for conspiracy in restraint of trade under the Criminal Code.
Is there anything to prevent them taking both proceedings?
No.

In the event of the board finding the parties guilty and the parties continuing in business, if they are indicted under the Criminal Code and convicted, would ther'e be an appeal from that conviction?
I am not familiar with the matter of appeals under the Criminal Code. But whatever the provisions of the criminal law may be as to appeals, they would continue to apply.

One would have thought that the Minister of Justice or som'e one else would have been at hand to instruct us on such a point as that, for it is very important. If a case has to run all the ordinary appeals of the courts up to the Supreme Court, how long would it take to get a conviction and reach a finality? It would be a long process.
On s'ection 25,
The proceedings of the board shall be conducted in public, but the board may order that any portion of the proceedings shall be conducted in private.
I think that clause should be eliminated. If you are going to have a public body examining evidence in the public interest, that examination should be held in public.
The board does sit in public.
But it may order that any portion of the proceedings shall be conducted in private. I think that ought to be amended.

It is apparent that it will require two members of the board to, give that decision. There may be cases where it is desirable to examine certain books, the contents of which it is not advisable to make public. I think that the board should be allowed some discretion in that matter. It is complain'ed that possibly this legislation may open the door to people prying into the business of others. I think that the chairman and one member of the board should have the power to order part of the inquiry to be made in private if they think necessary.

The answer may seem very apropos. But I do not think this country is Russia yet. We cannot advance the public interest by having secret trials. If there is to be a sweat-box, if manufacturers are to be given the third degree, let it be done in public. It shows very bad faith on the part of the department to wish to hold an investigation of this kind, at any stage, in private. Public trials, from the time of Magna Charta, 1 understand, have been held in public. And I think that is a good rule to hold by.

I would point out that this is a board of inquiry. After a party is found guilty, it might be right to give the evidence to the public, but, suppose that there is no guilt, why should a man who has done no wrong have the facts of his business made public? I do not think the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie) should apply any fine theories to this question. It seems to me that the minister is quite fair in this matter. Until the parties are

found guilty, there are many things that should be kept quiet.

The hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) may think so, but I do not think so, and I believe the public will agree with me rather than with him. I believe that the public will say that if a trial of a public character is to be held, it should be held openly. I think the day has gone by when we can adopt Eussian methods, hold courts in camera, hold a gun to the head of people to gain information from them unfairly-in other words, third degree, the thumbscrew and the boot; the use of methods that dare not be used in public. The interest of parties- on trial are far more secure in a public court than in a private inquiry.
I think the hon. member (Mr. J, A. Currie) is giving an interpretation to the section that it hardly deserves. Precisely the same section exists in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.

And it is wrong.
Mr. KING Boards of investigation are appointed similar to those under this Act, and it is found advantageous in many cases to allow the board to make private inquiry. I do* not think it is to be presumed, particularly when the chairman of the board is a judge of the court, one who is accustomed to administer the law, that he will, by his -own volition, go out of his way to see that a part of the proceedings are conducted in private unless it is very much in the public interest that they should be so conducted.
1 Mr. J. A. CUEEIE. I did not know that the chairman of the board should be 'a judge.
1 Mr. KING. Then the hon. gentleman has not read the Act. That is in section 12, that we have already enacted.

I still hold that the provision is unjust and unfair, and gives the minister and his department a *weapon, and a screw, and a means of squeezing everybody in this country that is in any kind of business. The thing is unjust, unfair and unBritish. If you are going to hold an inquest of any kind, hold it in public; don't be afraid, don't go into a hole and comer with it. The farming community will want to know what is at the bottom of these things; so don't let us adopt any of these Bus-sian methods. For my part I don't approve of them.

It seems to me the remarks- of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) are entirely uncalled for. I do not think there is anything Eussian in the proposed investigation. On the whole. I think the methods proposed will be in the Mr. NESBITT.
interest of the combinations of which the hon. gentleman seems to be the chief guardian here to-day. If there is any. combination whose affairs are being inquired into, it might be necessary to look into their books in order to find whether a combination existed, and it would not be just, or fair, or right to have their private affairs spread broadcast throughout the country. But if the investigation were allowed to take place in private, then the officials of the company or interest, with the books of the firm could be brought before the judge. There is no court in this land but permits a private investigation of that kind, and the results are not published. Why should it not be so in this case?
The hon. gentleman knows that under the Industrial Disputes Act there has never been any inquiry of this kind held.
Yes, out of the eighty inquiries several of them have been held in private.

I object to this clause as distinctly unBritish. It just shows the intent of this whole thing, which is to pry into private affairs, in the dark, to get down into the cellar, to dig things up, and make inquiries that the men on this board would not have courage to make in an open court. If you want justice you can always get it in open court, there is the place to get it. A court in camera as here proposed, an investigation in secret of this kind, to my mind, savors of Eussian methods, I have no hesitation in stating that to the minister. If this is a just provision, if any man can stand up and defend this Act, he should be able to defend it openly, as a machine that will work in the open, as an Act that can be defended at any stage, that this court is to be an open and just court, instead of a court held in the darkness, where the screws can be applied to people, and questions asked by the judges that they would not dare to ask in open court, and as I said before, apply detective methods to the accused, in other words, what is known as the third degree. That is what this Act intends, and unless the minister withdraws that provision I do not think he will receive very much credit from the public.
The remarks of the hon. gentleman are primarily a reflection upon the judiciary of this country

I fail to see it.
Mr. KING

because in each case two
members of the board must request that part of the proceedings should be held in private. Now the judge has to be a consenting party. As long as the judge is not a consenting party, the only alterna-

tive is that both the representative of the combine and the representative of the people who are preferring the complaint, must agree that part of the proceedings shall be in private. If they mutually agree that the public interest can be best served by carrying on part of the proceedings in private, then those proceedings would be held in private; if otherwise, the party desiring privacy would have to get the consent of the judge before that privacy could be observed; consequently the onus falls upon the judge, and hence the remarks of the hon. gentleman with regard to Russian methods constitute a reflection on the judiciary of this country which he is not entitled to make.

I object to the hon. minister trying to argue that my criticism constitutes a reflection on the judiciary. The clause says in effect that two members can order the court to be held in private. Now the two members, of whom the judge is not one, can order that court to be held in private. Is that not so?
I mentioned that.

Then why argue that I am insulting the judiciary when I am not? Two members who are not the judge can compel the court to be held in private against the will of the judge. So the argument of the minister falls completely to the ground. I have not cast any reflection on the judiciary, because the minister has acknowledged that any two members can order this court to be held in private without the consent of the judge. I claim there is no necessity for that whatever, and I will never sit silent and allow legislation to be passed here where any trial of any kind can be held in private. I think the more light there is thrown on any investigation of this kind, the better for the public, and the better for the people under control.

The hon. minister, in explaining this Bill said that one of its important features was publicity. But the very first sentence of this clause says:
The proceedings of the board should be conducted in public.

That clearly is the intention of the measure. But authority is given to the board to conduct a portion of the proceedings in private; that does not mean the whole proceedings, it simply give3 discretion to the board to hold a certain part of the proceedings in private. There can be only the alternatives for such privacy, either both the parties complaining and the party complained against must agree that it is best to conduct part of the investigation in private, and surely in that case it would be proper to have that part of the inquiry private. The other alternative is when one or both the representatives agree with the judge that part ought to be in private. It seems to me that in view of the nature of the questions that are being investigated, this provision in the Act is not open to criticism.
When the minister was explaining his Bill to the House, he said that one of the important features was publicity. Now he does not pretend to secure publicity when the case is being tried.

I might point out that, supposing you had the whole proceedings absolutely private, the finding of the board is always made public, and that is what will affect public opinion. The thing the public are interested in is to know whether certain men are combining, and whether they have done anytihng which affects the public interest detrimentally. The particular parts of the evidence upon which they base their judgment would certainly be given; the details of a man's business are a secondary consideration with the public.

The hon. member for Huron (Mr. McLean) said it was necessary to hold the inquiry in private in order that the books of the firm might be examined. 1 see that section 37 provides that the board may employ competent experts to examine books or official reports, but the information obtained therefrom should not be made public. Therefore there could be no object in holding this investigation in private when the board have already the right to use the information which they get from these experts.
Section 37 relates to an investigation made through experts, not to the investigation made by the board.

I am referring to the argument- of the hon. member for Huron (Mr. M. Y. McLean), that it would be necessary that that should be done in private, because it would involve the examination of books and records.

But the members of a board themselves might wish to examine those records. The section that he quotes refers to the examination by experts. That is a different thing. The board themselves may wish to examine some of the books, and they might wish to do that in private. If they wish to do it in private I think they should have the right to do so.

It- is within the recollection of people who are not very old, that there was a charge made of a combination amongst school-book manufacturers in Ontario, and a royal commission was appointed to investigate. It was permitted to hold its meetings in private. It held its meetings in private and reported that there was no combine amongst the manu-

facturers of school-books.. There was a change of government, another commission was appointed to investigate, it made its investigation in public and reported that there was a combination. I am strongly of the opinion that these investigations should be made in public. The minister cannot show any reason why there should be a dark lantern tribunal to carry on investigations of this kind.
On section 34, party may be compelled to give evidence.
Is not the word ' compelled,' a little strong?

If you take it out it may^ be impossible to get evidence from parties. That section is already a part of the Industrial Disputes Act, and it has not been found to work any injustice. A man might say:	I will refuse to answer any questions, and you could not proceed with the investigation.
On section 44, allowances determined by minister.
The clerk and others employed by the board will not be permanent? They will only be for the investigation?
Yes.
Will this provision with respect to allowances include the six persons making the complaint? They would certainly be at a loss of time and expense, and I think they should be remunerated in some way.

There is a section which allows the judge power to make disbursements, and under that section he would have the power to reimburse the six persons if he thought they were put to expense.
On section 48,

I wish to move as section 48 the following:
This Act shall not be construed to repeal or amend or in any way affect the Trades Union Act, chapter 125, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906.
To make plain the purpose of this section, I shall read the following letter which I have received from the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress:
Office of Secretary Treasurer,
Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
Ottawa, Ont., March 14, 1910. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, C.M.G.,
Minister of Labour,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Regarding Bill (No. 101) of this session, the Combines Investigation Act, introduced by you on January 18, we, the Executive Council of the Trades and Labour Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
Congress of Canada, representing various trade and labour organizations throughout Canada in re legislative enactments, have had the said Bill under careful consideration.
From the title of the Bill we gather that it is intended to apply only to such combines, monopolies and mergers as may enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of consumers. As the working classes compose the largest body of consumers we believe that they more than any other class in the community are likely to suffer the most through the enhancement of prices or anything that may prove of general detriment to consumers, and consequently they may be expected to view with favour any legislation which may result in the betterment of their conditions.
We realize that trusts and monopolies may become not merely a serious menace to consumers through the methods which they have sometimes employed to enhance prices, but that these powerful aggregations of capital may also become a serious menace to labour by their power where they have control of industrial establishments, to force unfavourable conditions upon workingmen, as well as producers and consumers, through the closing up of establishments or by other arbitrary methods of procedure, and we therefore feel that any measure which will secure publicity where such unfair methods are resorted to, cannot be other than of service to all classes in the community.
We are most anxious, therefore, that any legislation calculated to improve the condition of the working classes of this country should receive the support of parliament. At the same time we feel it most important that care should be taken to see that any rights and privileges secured to the working classes by past legislation should in no way be impaired. The Trades Union Act of 1872 which forms chapter 125 of the Revised Statutes of Canada was passed to secure to workingmen certain rights as members of trade unions. We do not think it is the intention of your Bill to, in any way, take away any rights already secured to labour by legislation. As, however, some doubt has been expressed on the possible effect of the measure in this respect, we think the intention of parliament in this particular should be made plain, and would, therefore, suggest the insertion of the following clause:-
This Act shall not be construed to repeal, amend, or in any way affect chapter 125 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, intituled:	' An
Act respecting Trade Unions.'
You will see that the insertion of such a clause gives to trade unions no new rights or privileges, but merely guarantees to them the enjoyment of rights which they have had by statute for some thirty-eight years.
Similarly, we will say that we do not think your Bill contemplates depriving organizations of capital of any rights which they may enjoy by statute, at the present time, nor do we think it should. Labour does not ask more than it is prepared to give.
Should, therefore, parliament see well to insert the safeguard herein suggested, we do not hesitate to say that the Bill would have the hearty endorsation of the organizations which we represent, and which are some 628

in number, and hare a total membership of 40,738.
Yours very respectfully,
(Ssd.) WM. GLOCKLING,
-	" GTJS. FRANCO,

Executive Council,
Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
The request seems to be a perfectly reasonable one, and I, therefore, beg to have the section I have moved added as one of the sections of the Bill.

Referring for a moment to a clause which has been passed already, I see you are proposing to amend the Tariff Act by this Bill. Can we properly amend the Tariff Act without the House being in Committee of Ways and Means?
All we are doing here is transferring one section of the Tariff Act from an existing Act to this legislation. We are not adding to it one way or the other.
You say in this Bill that one section of the Tariff Act is repealed, and in doing so you amend the Tariff Act. Can that be done without the House being in Committee of Ways and Means?

You cannot impose taxes without the House being in Committee of Ways and Means, but I suppose the House is at liberty to repeal taxes without that procedure. Is not the significance of the House going into Committee of Ways and Means that you are imposing taxes.
If that contention is right, then you could put a clause in this Bill repealing the whole of the Tariff Act, and no one would seriously pretend you could do that.

The point of the hon. gentleman might be of some importance in the matter of procedure providing we were attempting by this legislation 'to change materially the existing tariff in any part. We are not doing that at all. We are repealing one section of the tariff and inserting it in another part of this measure with the net result that the tariff stands in precisely the same position that it does to-day.
The question I ask is whether we can repeal a portion of the Tariff Act without going into Committee of Ways and Means.

FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 166) respecting insurance. He said: The House will remember that, at the last session of parliament, w'e had before us, and gave very much attention to, a Bill to revise and amend the Insurance Act. After the usual preliminary considerations, the Bill was referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, where public hearings were held and an opportunity afforded to all parties interested to present their views. Then, a sub-committee of the Banking and Commerce Committee was appointed, and the matter was taken up in detail and with great care by that subcommittee. The Bill in due course was reported to the committee and came before the House, where it was fully considered and then sent to the Senate. At that time,

the session was very far advanced, and the hon. gentlemen of the Senate, not unreasonably, thought that they ought to have further time for consideration of the measure, and so it was left over. In the present session the Bill was re-introduced in the Senate in substantially the form in which it had left the House of Commons last year. The S'enate has given it very great consideration-I think it not too much to say more than ordinary consideration, the hon. members for the Banking and Commerce Committee of the Senate having taken great interest in it. The Bill was passed with some amendments and is now before this House. Inasmuch as the House gave the measure such full consideration last session, I think I shall be right in saying that there will be no desire to go through the matter in detail again. But, if there is any need, attention may be called to important amendments made by the Senate. Some of the amendments, though useful, are not very important, but several of them are important. There was a clause in the Bill last year as it left this House, providing for what is called a gain and loss ^exhibit to be included in the annual statements of the companies. The Senate has made an amendment the effect of which is that that gain and loss exhibit shall not be required in the annual statement, but the Superintendent of Insurance shall have power to call for such statement whenever he thinks the affairs of the company render It necessary. Another amendment was on the question of bonuses to agents. The effect of the Bill as it left this House was to prevent the granting of bonuses. Tire Senate has amended the Bill so as to provide that bonuses shall not be forbidden, but they must be a matter of agreement. If bonuses are not agreed on in advance as part of the remuneration of the agent they may not b'e allowed. Another amendment is with respect to the policyholders' directors. Certain companies already provided for their policy-holders, as well as their stock-holders, having votes. It was proposed in the Bill that policyholders generally should be permitted to vote, and by proxy. The Senate has made an amendment in which they have recognized the right of policy-holders to vote, but they have denied the proxy vote to policy-holders.
Does that apply to fire insurance as well as life?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To life insurance. The changes are chiefly in the matter of life insurance. There was a provision respecting the annual election of directors, and it is proposed that a company may elect directors for one, two or three years, according to the by-laws of the company.
Perhaps the most important question
that was considered by the Senate was with respect to fire insurance-the insurance of property in unlicensed companies. The general purpose of the Act, of course, was to require that the insurance business of the country should be done in companies licensed under the Insurance Act. But it was claimed that a too rigid adherence to that principle would operate harshly upon some of the great property owners of the country. It was alleged that the existing companies in Canada were not able to handle all the insurance offered to them, and that sometimes the volume of insurance desired could not be obtained, apart altogether from the question of rates. It was further alleged that our Canadian companies had not adapted themselves to some sp'ecial forms of insurance which had been established in the United States. We compromised that matter in our Bill of a year ago by providing that insurance might be taken in unlicensed companies, provided that a record of such insurance was reported and a small tax paid on the business. There was a good deal of contention over that point, but I think that the Bill as it left the House was regarded, in that respect, as something of a compromise. However, that question was fully considered in the Senate. That House has made an amendment the substance of which is that business may be done with these unlicensed companies at the risk of the party who takes the insurance, but that the foreign companies which engage in that business, though they have the right to make these contracts abroad, shall not establish agencies in Canada, and shall not solicit the business. If a party in Canada desires to get insurance of that kind, he may send his order for it to the United States, may make his contract in the United States, at whatever risk is involved, but there shall be no penalty. But the company shall not be permitted to seek the insurance. If they send agents, or open agencies, or do anything to bring them into competition with the companies licensed in Canada, they will come under the provisions of the law which will forbid that business.
These are the chief amendments made by the Senate. So far as I am concerned, I am disposed to accept the position that the conclusions of the Senate in the matter have been reached after wise consideration. While I am willing to consider any amendment proposed by any hon. member, I am prepared to accept the Bill as it has come from the Senate.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
