For instance, my recollection is that Germany compelled the American companies to get rid of their American securities held for the safety of German policy-holders and buy German securities.

I would suggest that when we come to section 15 which deals with the question of deposits, we should be better able to discuss the question.
On section 11, license to provincial companies.

Is it the intention of the government to grant a license for two ot more provinces, but not for the whole Dominion, and, for that purpose to accept a smaller deposit than for a license for the whole Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A clause of the Bill soon to be taken up touches on that point.
On section 14, deposits of securities with minister; in case of foreign company; in case of limited license.

My attention has just been called, by one of the Toronto fire insurance companies, to this section, and, if the minister will allow it, I would like to have the section stand until I have an opportunity of speaking to him about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Consideration of section 14, postponed. [DOT]
On section 15, securities permissible; valuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change in that, but it touches the point referred to by my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie).

This section provides that the deposits shall be
(a)	in securities of or guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, or in securities of or guaranteed by any province of Canada; or in securities of or guaranteed by the United Kingdom or any British colony.
I do not know that the other colonies offer us any privileges in this respect.
(b)	If such company is incorporated in any foreign country in securities of or guaranteed by the government of such country.
I think that ought to be cut out. There is no reason why foreign government securities should be received as deposits. There are plenty of Canadian securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member may be mistaken in thinking that we have plenty of Canadian securities. There are times when the insurance companies have difficulty in obtaining satisfactory securities. To-day the whole tendency is to purchase government and municipal securities. They are very largely used. The percentage of foreign securities used is not great, but to provide that we shall not receive such securities would not be a wise step.
Mr. DANIEL, J notice that ordinary municipal debentures are not considered to be sufficiently safeguarded to be accepted as deposits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) will read the next section he will see that there is provision for accepting other securities if the treasury board is satisfied of their value.
Subsection 2 of section 16 refers to a fall in the value of these securities. What means is there for determining their value from time to time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The officials of the department keep track of the quotations
of these securities and wherever there is depreciation they see that the amount is made good by calling for further deposits.

The hon. minister said that only these securities are to be-used. But section 16 leaves the door wide open. The government may take the securities of the United States Steel 'Corporation as deposits if the treasury board say so. I am a good Canadian, and I believe that we should let charity begin at home in this matter. We have plenty of corporations growing up in the west with not too great a market for their securities. It is better for us to lend money to ourselves than to lend it to foreigners who come in here and hang up deposits of their sechrity, and crowd us into the foreign market to sell ours. I think the point I have taken is a good Canadian point, and that we ought to stick to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only foreign securities we accept are those of the highest value either government or national. The securities that are taken under that clause are all of the very highest character.
Have you a list of them here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can get them.
Better let that clause stand until we get the list.

While foreign securities might be accepted there are many other securities than those mentioned in this Act that would be regarded as valuable securities, and which might be accepted by the treasury board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The bulk of the securities will be Canadian government or municipal securities, and provincial securities; when they are available. But there are not many of these. It is largely a question of British government securities, and Canadian municipal securities. I might bring down a list to my hon. friend, and he may be assured that this class of securities are of the very best.

It has been suggested to me that many of these companies refrain from purchasing Ontario government securities just because there happened to be a little excitement over the Hydro-Electric Commission. If these companies were compelled to buy only Canadian securities, and place only Canadian securities on deposit, there will always be a good market at home, and the interest will be paid into our own country. If our own securities are displaced by foreign securities the interest is paid into a foreign country to build up a foreign country at the expense of ours. I think that clause ought to stand until we have a little further explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be glad at the next stage of the Bill to Dring down a list of the class of securities we have accepted under this clause, and my hon. friend will find they are the best class of securities. With regard to Ontario government securities there is no question in our department; we have several deposits of Ontario government securities, and are very happy to receive them.

Would you receive
municipal securities as well? Take a large and rich county where the securities are guaranteed by the council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We do receive that
class of securities, and have great quantities of them.
Subsection 2 would give you that power, but it does not include municipal securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 16 gives that power.

I may say for the information of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), that municipal securities are deposited. They are bought from municipalities by commission agents at 94 and 95, and they are hung up on deposit in this department at cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, I am advised, is mistaken. These securities are accepted by us at their fair market value, and as a rule with a safe margin. There is no such thing, as my hon. friend thinks, of our accepting securities at a higher value. The great trouble is that the companies think we are rather too severe in our valuation and do not give them a high enough quotation.
On section 25, duplicates to be filed in office of a superior court.
What do these agencies mean? I understood that foreign companies were not to have agencies for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Foreign companies on being duly licensed may have agencies in Canada. What I said has reference .to these unlicensed companies which are permitted to do business under exceptional circumstances as previously mentioned; but ordinary foreigners taking out a license may do business like Canadian companies.

Supposing a company has its chief agency in Montreal, and a suit is brought in the province of Ontario : has the service to be made in Montreal, and would the suit have to be tried in Montreal or in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed the suit might still be brought in Ontario and be subject to Ontario laws.
On section 28, notice of ceasing of business.
The giving of notice shall be a condition precedent to the release of a company's deposit, but you release the deposit before they have fulfilled their contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, provision is made further on. The company's deposit will not be released until its liabilities in Canada have been met.
On section 31, paragraph (9), form of statements during 1910.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There i3 a slight change. The Bill as passed before provided that certain changes made by the superintendent in the annual statement might be subject to alteration by the minister. That has been changed. The statements as prepared by the superintendent shall be final and the minister shall not alter them. I think it is the better form.
It says in subclause 8 of section 31 ' the minister or superintendent ' may make changes. Either may do it.

___I think the minister
should be responsible for those changes. He is the responsible party, and the superintendent acts under the minister. I do not see any necessity^ for the superintendent being empowered to make changes without consultation with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not important. These are really technical matters, and it means that the minister would only initial what is recommended by the superintendent. So that if you have the superintendent's signature in the matter you have all that is of real value. If you had the minister's initials added, it would not add much to the value.
If the minister does something wrong, he is responsible to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to promise that I will not.	1
I understood from the minister that it was changed so as to place the responsibility entirely on the superintendent. That is not the alteration as it is printed here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the Bill as it passed the House it was provided that ' any 3uch change made by the superintendent shall be subject to alteration or cancellation by the minister.' These last "words have been stricken out; so that as it stands now it

is the superintendent's view and not the minister's which prevails.
Mr BARKER, Either can dc it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but in the event of the superintendent doing it and the minister being dissatisfied he had the right to change it. The Senate have stricken that out. I do not think it makes much difference. It is a technical matter, and the superintendent is the qualified officer to deal with it.
On section 36, time up to which annual statements are. made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was from section 36 that the provision with respect to gain and loss exhibit was stricken out, to which I have already called attention.
On section 37, superintendent and his duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not making any change here; we are simply filling in the salary of the superintendent as it exists under the law to-day. That could not be done in the Senate. We propose to fill the blank with the words 'five thousand dollars per annum,' so that it shall read ' not exceeding five thousand dollars per annum.'
That would come under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, deputy ministers, in a sense, do come under that in a special way. The superintendent of insurance has the rank of a deputy and is appointed under the same conditions.
I mean his retiring allowance and all that sort of thing; they would be considered under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Does not the Civil Service Act provide what the salary of a deputy is? You appear to have authority here to change that by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it says, 'not exceeding.'
But this gives you power to change that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has always been fixed in the Insurance Act, and the salary is that of a deputy. At the time this was fixed the deputies were paid a less sum. It is, in effect, the same thing; the superintendent is receiving the salary of a deputy.
Under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has always been fixed under the Insurance Act. Does my
hon. friend mean that we can make it less than $5,000?

No, but either one or the other authority should prevail. If he comes under the Civil Service Act, and if the Civil Service Act provides that a deputy shall get a certain amount, why should vou take authority to change that amount? I am not objecting to the amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not affect the present officer. If we were appointing a new officer and desired to do so we could give a less salary than $5,000, but he has by the Act the rank and position of a deputy.
How much does the Civil Service Act provide as the minimum amount that a deputy may receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Well, the Civil Service Act provides $5,000 as the minimum?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a fixed sum, not a minimum. The two Acts differ to this extent that we could appoint a superintendent of insurance at less than $5,000, and he could have a gradual rise to $5,000.
Does not the Civil Service Act cover all deputy heads under the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Then if it does, and if it says that a deputy head shall get so much, I do not see how you can take authority by order in council to change the words of the statute, because it is a statute.
This section gives them the authority.

I think the minister should allow the law with relation to the Civil Service to stand as it is and not take power to fix the salary at less than that provided for by the Civil Service Act. I do not think it is well for us to start, so soon after passing the Civil Service Act, to make changes. These things should work automatically.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not making changes. This is following the Insurance Act as it' has always been.

But we have initiated a new system under the Civil Service Act, and this is not a special service. Why should there be any change? We establish a bad precedent, because whenever a Bill comes un there will be changes made in some way or somebody will be demanding changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an apparent clash between the two Acts. This permits us to appoint a superintendent of insurance

at a less sum than $5,000 and then to raise it to $5,000. On the -other hand, the superintendent of insurance is a technical officer, and if the present officer were to retire, I do not think it would hurt very much to have the right to appoint another officer at a lower rate and let him go up in a year or two. At all events, it is on the side of economy.
On section 41, report when assets become insufficient; Governor in Council may suspend license of company; effect of suspension.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a change here providing that in the case of a company's license being cancelled a modified or additional license may be issued for the purpose of protecting the policy-holders of the company.
Should there not be a special arrangement whereby a special officer of the government should be put in charge to liquidate these assets; instead of sending it to the courts of big expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, I don't think we want to take that upon ourselves.
Do I understand that the superintendent can grant this modified or additional license and not the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
There must be a mistake there; I do not think the superintendent should have that power. It seems to me it is the minister who should grant the license.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That amendment was put in by the Senate, but I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Perley) is- right in saying that the minister should grant the license. We had better change that.
On section 42, basis of valuation-deduction from value of policies.
.Mr. PERLEY. This is a highly technical matter, and I would like to know if the clause as it has passed the Senate is practically the same as that passed by the House last session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Substantially it is. There has been some change in the wording, but it is not material.
I would like the minister to explain subsection 2 as to the basis of valuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to let my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) take that on trust. That is a technical matter, and the only explanation I could give would be to read the clause and my hon. friend would not be any better off then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The government through its officials fix the amount of the bonus or addition, under the British tables. Will these tables govern the companies apart altogether from the contract?
This simply deals with the guarantee each company has to put up and it is fixed in the British life tables.
You mean the reserve.
Yes, the reserve or guarantee, that is absolute in the policy. The profits are estimated by the company and in this Act we do not deal with profits at all.
Was this provision the outcome of a proposition by the insurance companies or is it the idea of the deputy minister for the protection of the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been a change in the tables accepted as the standard,- but otherwise this is a continuation of what has been in the Insurance Act for years. The change in the tables has been suggested by the department because it is a more modem table and deemed to be a better basis of computation.
Do you provide that all policies after 1900 shall be on this basis and that policies before 1900 would be on whatever basis the company had followed previously?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The basis is the same, the variation is only in the rate of interest.

The minister and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) have failed to catch the point. The superintendent of insurance goes into the office of the insurance company and says:	You are charging too low a premium; you must chaTge a certain premium; and that becomes law-the company has to charge that. He goes to value the policies -of the company, and he finds that it has been paying too much in the way of bonus or addition out of profits, and he says: That is contrary to this table; this is the amount you must fix as the amount of your bonus to policy-holders. By this clause it appears to me that the government is taking upon itself, through its superintendent, to fix the amount of bonus that the companies shall pay. I grant that it is a matter of contract, but the superintendent-having such wide powers enabling him virtually to vary contracts so far as premiums are concerned, will this clause be construed as enabling him to vary the profits or bonuses payable to policy-holders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the bonus is not determined by the superintendent. He has

*to take what the company establishes as the bonus, but that becomes an element in the valuation. The superintendent has nothing to do with establishing what the bonus or the amount of the profits shall be.

I do not think the minister is right in saying that the rate of interest shall be the basis of the valuation. There are the two elements-the rate of interest at 34 per cent and these tables; that is, in regard to all policies issued after 1900. Policies issued before that may have been on a different basis.

They were on a different interest basis. The British life table is simply an experience table, and the companies put up so much yearly of an absolute guarantee and add 34 per cent of interest to that. Previous to 1900 it was 4 per cent.
Upon what basis was the valuation?
It may have been on the healthy male table. The guarantee is absolute.

Suppose a party were dropping out of the company. He must be settled with on some basis, and the company is earning profits. On what basis will these profits be declared? On the British offices life tables of 1893, or on what basis? I take it that this clause would disturb contracts which have been entered into with the Canada Life Company, and to that extent probably interfere with the litigation that is going on at the present time. Would or would not this clause interfere with the rights of policy-holders which might be determined under that litigation?
This would not interfere, because the higher the guarantee the less the profit. The Canada Life, like all other companies, was forced after 1900 to guarantee on a higher basis.
The profits the companies earned before that time were higher than they have been since, and they have robbed the policy-holders of those profits.
I think the Act provides a standard policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a clause that every policy shall contain certain conditions but that comes later in the Bill.

I think that this subsection would mean that where there is
any departure from the standard in issuing a policy it will be a violation.
On section 47, contributions of certain companies towards office expenses.
Suppose a company refuses to do what is provided for here, what can you do, except cancel its license?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is all we can do, suspend its license to do business in Canada. There is no other penalty.
On section 52, change of head office and date of annual meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a somewhat lengthy clause. It provides machinery for amalgamation and transfer. Some changes have been made. I will read the memorandum.
This section was originally drafted along the lines of the corresponding section in the English Companies Act. In the Act passed at the last session of the imperial parliament, however, a few changes were made, and these changes have also been made in this section.
The changes are to correspond with those made in the English Act.
What are the changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A few words here and there. Paragraph 3, subsection, as amended, requires that in a case of reinsurance or amalgamation, notice of the transfer shall be served on the shareholders and policyholders of both companies, instead of on the shareholders and policy-holders of the re-insured company alone as originally provided.
Suppose that the treasury board do not agree to it, can the government compel that company to go into liquidation and use the money forwarded to them for distribution among the policyholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government would have to refuse the license and that would force the company into liquidation.
That would be a very grave step.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not be done unless there is a strong need for it.
On section 54, advances to agents.
Might I ask the minister whether they did not change that somewhat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section has been amended by removing the restriction of advances on first year's tpremiums and providing that advances may be made without restriction, but that such advances shall not be allowed as assets in the superintendent's report. In subsection 2, exempt-

ing industrial companies from the provision of the section, has also been struck out, as the amendment in subsection 1, rendered this exemption unnecessary.
On section 55, salaries of officers and agents.
Will the minister explain what change there is in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In substance I am told there is no change, though there has been redrafting. As the section, as amended, stands, it affects only contracts to be entered into hereafter.
On section 56, salary agreement, for not more than five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has been changed to provide that the time for which an agreement between a company and its officers or trustees may be made shall not exceed five years instead of ten years, as in the old section.

Does that affect the contracts made with agents? I understand that a great many agents have contracts with the companies made years ago under which they were to receive a certain portion of the annual premium. These men worked hard for years and got a large business for their companies, land have retired expecting that these renewal commissions will be paid them. Does this affect them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This Bill will not interfere with that.
On section 57-commissions to agents only: pension fund may be created.
Who gets that pension? It is spoken of as a ( staff pension fund.' Who are the ' staff'? Do they include the directors or the agents, or does this mean the office staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would take it to mean the head office staff.
I am not raising objection, but I think that should be defined in such a way that there may be no misconstruction.
It might include the president.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, he would be the head of the office staff.
Is that intended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The scheme must be submitted to the general meeting of the members. If they approve it, I do not see why we should prevent it.
On section 59, investment of company's funds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Several amendments have been made in the investments section. Under subsection (a) of section 1 is added ' or guarantee by any municipal corporation in Canada.' Paragraph 3 of subsection (b) has been amended so as to provide that the stocks of a company guaranteed by a company which has paid regular dividends upon its preferred or common stock for not less than five years will be accepted for investment. This puts the stock of the company that is guaranteed on the same footing as that of the guaranteeing company. It accepts the guarantee as equivalent to the original stock.
This opens a very-wide door. A company with a capital stock of $10,000 on which it has paid dividends might guarantee the stock of a half million dollar company, and thus make that stock eligible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be an abuse of the Act. I would ask that that section be allowed to stand for further consideration of paragraph 3-not the whole. We will think of the point raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie).

It is right to let it stand, but the minister ought to promise us that the matter shall be set right, for it might come up when we are not here and pass without being amended. A ten-thousand dollar company should not be allowed to guarantee a million dollars of another company's stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will consider that. The hon. member (Mr. Perley) knows the spirit in which the Bill has been dealt with, and may feel sure that the matter will receive full consideration.
And the minister will improve it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Either that or attention will be called to it in the House. Whatever decision we reach will be conveyed to the House. In paragraph 4 of subsection (b) the provision was that not more than twenty per cent of the common stocks and not more than twenty per cent of the total issu'e of the stock of any company shall be purchased by any life insurance company. That has been changed to thirty per cent. It was pointed out that, as the field of stock investment is very limited in Canada, the companies should not be so much restricted. It was pointed out that there is no danger of the control passing to the investing company when only thirty per cent of the stock is permitted to be purchased.
Subsection 3 is replaced with a new subsection, to 'enable a company to obtain the securities of a company for reorganiza-

tion if the securities of that company were previously owned by the insurance company.

In connection with the matter of guarantee to which we have b'een alluding, the Minister of Finance might consider whether such investments might not be subject to the approval of the Treasury Board instead of being as large as they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I promise to look into that.

This subsection 3 allows the Treasury Board to authorize the
acceptance by a company of securities not fulfilling the foregoing requirements of the section in payment or part payment for securities sol'd by the company. If the securities they receive are not such as are authorized by the Act, I suppose they would have to sell them within five years under the previous section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if unauthorized, they would have to be sold within five years.
Even those that the Treasury Board allowed them to take under this subsection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we accept them they would become good.

That is exactly the point I am making. Under subsection 3, the Treasury Board may authorize the acceptance of thes'e securities in payment or part payment for securities held by the company. That is, securities they are not allowed to take under this x\ct might be authorized by the Treasury Board. They ought to be obliged to sell them within a reasonable time. If the Treasury Board allowed them to take these securities which they could not get in any other way, that should not allow them to keep them for ever.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They would still be subject to the clause that they must be sold within a reasonable time.
On section 60, deposits outside of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In subsection 1 the words ' and securities ' have been inserted after the word ' funds,' in order to make it clear that a company might deposit securities outside of Canada. It was considered that it would be unreasonable to refuse permission for the temporary removal of securities from Canada.

That is a proper change; but I object to the word ' person,' being used in the last line. It seems to me in these days when we have trust companies and banks, that a person should not be
authorized to receive these securities for purposes of exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A person would include a corporation.
I do not think any individual should be allowed to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is one of the Senate's new clauses, and that may also stand. Of course it would not prevent us using a bank or trust company for the purpose, but it would allow an individual. We will look into that.
Would the trust company not charge a commission, and an individual might do it without commission?
An insurance company would have to pay any charges of that kind. If the word ' person ' were changed to a responsible bank or trust company, it would answer my objection.

Is it at all likely that the department would put them in with a person that is not responsible? It says ' a responsible person.' I think the clause is good as it stands.
On section 67, holding of real estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
An amendment has been made to this section providing that a company may acquire and hold such real estate in the United Kingdom as is necessary for the maintenance of its branches there, provided that the consent of the treasury board to the acquisition has been obtained. This amendment was supported by the argument that it would increase the companies' standing in the eyes of the British insurance public.
On section 76, voting by proxy, companies other than life.
Is the Independent Order of Foresters counted an assessment company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. There is a change in section 76, as it passed this House, when subsection 4 provided that a proxy shall not be valid unless it is executed within three months prior to the meeting in which the same is to be used. I have a memorandum stating that subsection 4, requiring that a proxy of the mutual companies must be executed within three months, is struck out, since policy-holders' proxies have been abolished in section 98, and there seems no reason for imposing this limitation on mutual companies.
Then the proxy is good for ever?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is good until revoked. The policy-holders have no proxy.
On section 77, investments, annual report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section has been amended. It empowers the superintendent to disallow such investments as he considers unauthorized by the Act, and provides for an appeal to the Exchequer Court against his decision. The companies claimed that pending the result of such appeal, the superintendent's ruling should be suspended, and an amendment has been made to subsection 4, providing that if the company gives notice of its intention to appeal within fifteen days of being notified of the superintendent's ruling, and within fifteen days thereafter files its appeal with the registrar of the Exchequer Court, the superintendent's ruling shall be suspended until the judgment of the Exchequer Court has been rendered. This will give the company thirty days within which to file its appeal. The section has also been amended to provide for its coming into force on January 1, 1911.
On section 79, reduction and subsequent increase of capital.
Is the provision with respect to the reduction of capital the same as in the old Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The question raised by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is a pertinent one. Could a company whose capital is not all paid up, when trouble is apprehended, write off its stock and release its shareholders from liability?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the liability remains.
It is paid up capital that it has power to reduce under section 79.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Read subsection 4.
On section 80, increase of capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The first line of section 80 has been amended by providing that only that portion of the profits of the company which belongs to the shareholders shall be used for increasing the capital stock.
Is there a clause which provides that the list of securities held by a company shall be at the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That comes in the annual statement submitted by the company to the department.
On section 87, rebates, discrimination, etc., forbidden.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a change in 87, but it is not material.

87 has been altered?
Mr,. FIELDING. The alterations are only verbal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -Mr. NESBITT. I would like to ask the minister that subsection 2 of section 87, should stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right.
Subsection 2 of section 87 allowed to stand.
Does the provision in section 85, that the agent of the company is not to be the agent of the insured apply to fraternal companies as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.
On section 90, surplus under deferred dividend policies.

I notice that the figures are to be taken every fifth year with regard to a deferred policy. Would it not he better for each company to have a set time for reckoning the profits on such policies, having the company's year instead of the policy's year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the clause as we passed it before, and I think no question was raised as to its suitability.

On this question of the quinquennial payments, would it not be possible to have company periods. Could not it be worked out on a five years' computation. I think every company should have its quinquennial period to suit itself, with adjustments made for five years, and not to have each policy made up every five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All the policies would be valued at the same time?
Yes, and to meet the intermediate policies there could be an adjustment.
That is done now.
My impression is that that is now done by the companies.

It is the net profit that is divided, and to my mind the only, way to work that out from an actuarial-standpoint would be to have a five year company period. The company has its great clearing house every five years and makes an adjustment on the policies accordingly.
That is what they do now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that what my hon. friend from Hamilton suggests is the rule of practice now.
That is probably what the Act seem3 to contemplate.
But it is not so expressed.

Each company has its quinquennial period, and if any policy

falls in between the periods they give them their proportion.
This section <ioe3 not contemplate that.
I think it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it means what the hon. gentleman desires.

Yes, but it does not set forth what it means.
On section 95, form of policy to be approved-days of grace for payment of premiums-incontestability after two years- policy and endorsement to be entire contract-age understated-lapsed policies- loan on policy-table of surrender and loan values-table of instalments-renewal of policy-exceptions.
Is there a change in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. In paragraph (g) the Bill as introduced provided that all loan agreements on policies must be made on a fixed form. Several of the companies pointed out this would cause great inconvenience to the companies, and it was decided that the company's own form should be allowed to be used, subject to the approval of the superintendent. An amendment has been made in accordance with this suggestion.
Why do you make it compulsory under clause 94 for the party to get the acquiescence of the superintendent to institute a suit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: His individual right to bring suit against the company would remain, but in the case of the Attorney General being applied to to bring a suit for some public interest, the superintendent should be applied to.
I cannot see that the companies can give any reasonable excuse why they should not use the government forms.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If an approved form is used, the public interest is protected.
I am glad to know these forms have to be submitted to the superintendent, because the companies have had a grievance wdth reference to these company forms.
Colonel Worthington made a reference to the war risks on militiamen. What- is to be done about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Deserving as the object is, I do not see how we can legislate in such a matter.

I think an amendment could be inserted in subclause (b)
stating that the amount of that extra war' payment should be printed on the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are big wars and little wars, and I think the company would desire to have an opportunity of varying the rates,in accordance with the risks that may arise. We have not had any representation that there has been any difficulty under the existing law7 in that Tespect.
The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) suggested an amendment to subsection (b) of section 95, which I would like the minister to take under advisement, holding this subsection over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very good.
The companies all have in their policies now the amount additional they charge for war risks.
If they have, it might as well be put in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have the impression that war risks may vary in their quality and character.
On section 96, separate accounts of participating and non-participating business.

What is the idea of having separate accounts for participating and non-participating policies? The companies limit the profits for participating policy-holders to the participating business, while the profits on the non-participating business I suppose go to the shareholders. This is one of the grievances that were up before. A man who takes out a participating policy understands that he participates m all the profits of the company in a certain proportion along with the share-holders. Most of the companies as a matter of fact only allow to the participating policyholder the profits that accrue from participating policies. The keeping of these two accounts separate makes it all the more easy for the companies to do this.

The companies issue nonparticipating policies at a very much lower premium than participating policies; and this clause has been inserted for the purpose of enabling the companies to withdraw from the participating policy-holders a sufficient amount to make up for the lack of premiums paid by the non-participating policy-holders.
On section 98, shareholders' and policyholders' directors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There have been some changes made in this section. It is one to which the committee of the Senate gave very much time. The decision of the committee with respect to the representation of policy-holders on the board of directors may be summarized as follows:

1.	Policy-holder are to be allowed to have representation on the board.
2.	The total number of directors is to be not less than nine nor more than fifteen (the original section had nine and sixteen).
3.	The policy-holders5 directors must be. at
least one-third of the board (last year's section had two-fifths).	*
1. The directors of both classes may be elected for one, two, or three years.
5.	If elected for two or three years they may according as determined by the company's by-laws-
(a)	hold office continuously for the full term, or
(b)	a certain proportion retire annually.
6. Policy-holders are not allowed to vote by proxy.
7.	The qualifications for policy-holders voting and acting as directors have been left the same as in last year's Bill.
An amendment has been made to subsection 7, providing that a policy-holder as a member of a company shall not in case of liquidation be liable to be placed op the list of contributories, or to share in the distribution of assets. Subsection 11 has been changed to provide that the date of the holding of the annual meeting shall be printed on every renewal receipt issued by the company, instead of the company being obliged to serve every policy-holder with a special notice of the annual meeting. Subsections 13 and 14 have been consolidated into a new subsection 13. These in general terms are the different proposals from the Senate.

I would like to ask the minister whether a point which was much discussed last year has been dealt with,
that is, whether a shareholder can sit as a policy-holder's director?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, as proposed now, he cannot.
The policy-holder's director must be interested simply as a policyholder?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Why should not a policyholder vote by proxy as well as a shareholder?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was one of those who thought he should; but in this matter I am willing to accept the judgment of the Senate rather than delay the Bill.

I agree with the minister that the policy-holders should elect their own directors. I do not see why they should not have the same privilege in that respect as the shareholders. Apparently there is a clear line of cleavage between the director who represents the shareholders and the director who is to represent the policy-holders. The policyholders should have the same freedom of electing their director as the shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the judgment of this House would sustain the minister on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that one of the arguments that influenced the Senate was the expense that would be involved. Of course, there are an immense number of policy-holders, and the cost of issuing proxies to those would be very large. However, rather than delay the Bill, I am willing to accept the Senate's compromise.
I do not see why the date of the annual meeting should not be put on the policy, unless it is left in this way because they might want to change the date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They might want to change it.
On section 102, companies ceasing to do business.
There are some companies which formerly did business in this country and whose business is not yet wound up. Is there any change in this clause that would affect them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is the same clause as was in the Bill of last year. There is no change. It is the same as the existing law I am advised.
On section 102, companies ceasing to do business-winding up old business,
I would like to ask whether the public has the right to see the list of securities held by the government on deposit for these insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You mean the deposits held by the department?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no objection at any time to anybody obtaining that information who desires it.
A friend of mine is interested in this winding up, and he has been harshly dealt with, by the New York Mutual Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mutual reserve, you mean?

Yes, the Alutual Reserve. The procedure in those cases is this:	The government holds a certain
amount of security and deposits. As I understand the securities held by the government in the case of insurance companies are for the benefit of the parties who hold the insurance and for the purpose of renewing their insurance, that is their unearned premiums. Now in the case of this company, the moment their trouble arose, a Canadian gentleman, who is very active in assignee work applied to the courts to be appointed the assignee. About the same time an American assignee applied to be

assignee of the company in New York, and there was a conflict between them. The Canadian issued notices asking the policy-holders to send their policies and payments to him and the American did likewise. Some of the Canadians paid their premiums to the Canadian official before he was finally appointed by the courts, and it appears that some of those who paid to this Canadian official before his final appointment, have been deprived of the benefits to which they are entitled under this Act. In the case of those who paid to the American liquidator, their payments held good and their policies were not cancelled, while one or two who paid to the Canadian liquidator were cast out and have no redress. I think the minister should take that matter under advisement. I would like to know from the minister before this Bill passes, what amount of money on deposit in the department has been used for the payment of legal expenses and assignees' expenses in this matter, because if I know anything about these assignees, and especially about the gentleman in question, about one-third of the money held by the government will be swallowed up in expenses before the matter is settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have some reason for feeling interested in that company, but I am afraid the trouble was that my hon. friend's friend had a worthless policy, and was sad because he could not get something out of it.
You are absolutely wrong. It was nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There were so many like that that I naturally thought my friend's case was in that position. However, we have no record of the amount that was expended for legal expenses, but no doubt that will come to us later. The department did not undertake to distribute this money at all. It is purely a matter for the courts, and whatever money was in the hands of the government has been paid over to the liquidator by order of the court.
How long ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In August, 1908.

And this liquidator has deliberately dragged the settlement of that company's affairs along all this time and the minister allows it. The liquidator will not report for three or four years until he has eaten up all the money, i think there should be a limit to these matters and I intend to bring up the question again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter for the court, not for the department.

There ought to be something in this Act that would prevent anything of that kind. It should provide that when a company has to go into liquidation an inspector from the department should supervise it, the same as is done in connection with the banks in the United States, and the insurance companies there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department has enough to do without taking that on its shoulders. The hon. member's faith in the department is very acceptable to me, but I would rather trust the courts.

The liquidator would be an official of the court, but an outside man who has nothing to do with the company can now apply to a high count judge who is possibly also his friend and get the high court judge to say that he is to be the liquidator. He is appointed liquidator and he demands the money deposited with the government and applies it to his own private business as a trust fund or applies it as he likes. There should be some method whereby an official of the government could act as liquidator, of course, under the jurisdiction of the court; but an assignee who can get somebody to go on his bond has a right under this law to apply for a winding up order, to get all this money which the stockholders had deposited in the hands of the minister, have it paid to his own credit, and then his account is not settled for three or four years. I think it is time in the interests of the public and the policy-holders that something should be done in the way of appointing a supervisor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This assignee cannot get this money out of the hands of the government; the only people who can get it is the court, and if an order of the court requires us to give the money to the assignee, then the court is responsible.
Well, the minister will ascertain what the figures are and let me know what the cost of this liquidation has been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there is any record of it,
The minister has the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The court has the money; we have not.

I thought the minister said that the court came to the minister and got it dollar by dollar as it was needed. As a matter of fact if the court gave an order this man could draw half a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The court directed that whatever moneys were in the hands of the government should be paid over to the

assignee. The official was so paid and so far as we are concerned that was the end of it.
A moment ago the minister suggested that this money was paid out on the application of the assignee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing of the sort.
I say that an irresponsible assignee can come and get all the moneys here on deposit at the department, and hang up the settlement for four or five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is mistaken. An irresponsible assignee cannot get a penny of the money. An order of the court only can get the money.
What is the use of begging the question? All the court does is to instruct the assignee to go and get the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the court instructs the Minister of Finance to pay over the money, as we are good citizens and try to obey the orders of the court, we deliver the goods.
On section 109, reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to have that section stand, please.
On section 110, profits from participating policies to be kept distinct from other profits-rights of participating policy-holders to profits.

speechtext: Very good.
We have spent a long day, and I think it would be well that we should rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very well.
Can the minister tell us when it is likely that this Insurance Bill will come up again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not to-morrow. I can hardly say more than that. I want the superintendent of insurance and his officers to look over the various suggestions that have been made before we take the Bill up again.
